articles.title: Amazon Is Ratcheting Up Its Fight With NYC Delivery Drivers
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content: New Yorkers opening Amazon’s app on Thursday were greeted with a warning: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” A link invited them to “act now to protect low prices,” directing customers to contact their city council members about legislation that would require Amazon to directly employ its delivery drivers. Amazon rolled out the warnings, which also appear on packages delivered in the New York area, as part of its campaign against New York City’s Delivery Protection Act (DPA), which an Amazon-funded coalition has already spent upward of $8 million opposing. Amazon is warning customers that the legislation would put small delivery companies out of business, eliminate jobs, and delay their packages. The company has not explained how it calculated the additional $5 per order. The act’s partisans say Amazon’s threats are absurd. “The Delivery Protection Act would require companies like Amazon to pay a $500 licensing fee every other year and comply with workplace and public safety regulations,” Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s lead sponsor, told Jacobin . “It’s simply dishonest to claim that this bill would require them to charge consumers $5 for every delivery. New Yorkers won’t let themselves be bullied by corporations and billionaires.” “It’s a slap in the face to hardworking people everywhere,” Tony Rosario, a New York–based organizer for the Teamsters Amazon Division, told me. “You have to have some nerve to try to blame the city council for holding Amazon accountable.” He dismissed the company’s threats to leave the city should the legislation pass. “They’re not leaving New York City,” he said. The city is largely thought to be the company’s biggest market in the country. Mayor Zohran Mamdani also responded to the warnings Thursday afternoon. “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council’s efforts to protect workers’ rights and keep our streets safe,” he tweeted . “It’s greed.” Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash similarly used their apps to campaign for California’s Proposition 22 in 2020, spending more than $200 million to pass a measure allowing them to continue treating drivers as independent contractors. The legislation Amazon is fighting in New York would change who employs its sprawling delivery-driver workforce. Cabán’s bill would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to employ their drivers and warehouse workers directly. Amazon currently contracts out much of that work to smaller companies known as Delivery Service Partners (DSPs). The bill would also impose licensing, safety, and training requirements on delivery facilities, with protections for workers whose jobs are affected by the change. Thirty-four of the fifty-one City Council members have signed on as sponsors, and Mayor Mamdani supports the bill. Council Speaker Julie Menin, however, has yet to bring it to a vote. Councilmembers are negotiating changes to the legislation, including whether to retain the ban on subcontracting, which Amazon is particularly determined to defeat. When the company began planning its own delivery network in 2013, executives worried that entering the transportation business would expose it to organized labor. “A primary concern was whether getting into the transportation business would expose them to unions,” executives involved in those discussions told journalist Brad Stone. When Amazon launched the DSP program several years later, it could run its own delivery network while leaving the drivers on someone else’s payroll. The Teamsters have spent years fighting to establish that Amazon is a joint employer of those drivers and therefore has to bargain with their union. Amazon has threatened to challenge the DPA in court, and the bill is now fueling a steady stream of criticism in the right-wing New York Post . But the legislation could still pass without the requirement that Amazon directly employ its drivers. The current version of the bill would spare workers years of litigation at the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) to establish that Amazon is their employer and therefore must bargain with their union. That wouldn’t guarantee a collective bargaining agreement, but it would eliminate one of the company’s principal defenses against unionization. Amazon has funded its multimillion-dollar lobbying and advertising campaign through the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, which operates publicly as New York Delivers. Its advertisements feature DSP owners and drivers warning that the legislation would eliminate small businesses and raise prices. Amazon says that more than forty DSPs in New York City employ over five thousand workers whose jobs could be threatened if the companies were prohibited from contracting with Amazon. The company has also raised the possibility of moving delivery facilities outside city limits. The Teamsters’ Rosario said the concern is misplaced — and that the bill could help DSP owners too. “They’re being squeezed just as much as their employees are,” he said. DSP owners are responsible for maintaining and repairing vehicles and bear much of the responsibility when drivers are injured or involved in accidents. Under the existing arrangement, Rosario said, DSPs serve as a “scapegoat” for the company. Opposition to the bill includes the city’s chambers of commerce and the National Urban League, which has argued that the legislation would particularly harm black-owned delivery businesses. Amazon is listed among the organization’s highest-tier corporate donors, a category representing contributions of at least $1 million. On November 16, the National Urban League and the Amazon-backed New York Delivers coalition threatened legal action if the bill passes in its current form. Their attorney argued that the legislation conflicts with federal and state law. An earlier memo prepared by Brendan McGuire, an attorney at WilmerHale retained by the Amazon-funded Five Borough Jobs Campaign, argued that the bill could violate federal restrictions on local regulation of motor carriers. Menin, who supported an earlier version of the bill, has held off on backing the current one. She has raised concerns about potential job losses, higher prices for consumers, and whether the legislation would survive a legal challenge. A spokesman for the Mamdani administration’s Law Department told The New York Times that he was confident the final legislation would withstand legal scrutiny. The Times also reported that Menin has considered a version of the bill that would license and regulate delivery warehouses without requiring Amazon to directly employ its drivers, though she has not ruled out retaining the subcontracting ban. The New York Post reports that councilmembers are considering requiring warehouse operators to own the delivery vehicles currently owned or leased by contractors. Other details are still being negotiated, including how large a warehouse must be to fall under the law. Sources familiar with the negotiations expect the text to be finalized next week. “Direct employment is one of the most important provisions of the bill,” Rosario said. He said there had been some discussion of exceptions for truly independent contractors but was adamant that Amazon shouldn’t be exempt from the direct-employment requirement. “There’s no way they’re getting around that language,” he said. Menin has insisted that the council will regulate Amazon while protecting jobs and consumer prices. On Thursday, she criticized the company’s new direct appeals to customers. “It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote on X. “We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.” “If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong,” she added. The Teamsters called Amazon’s warnings to customers “extortion by one of the richest corporations in human history” and accused the company of caring about neither its workers nor its customers. The legislation has attracted support from across New York City’s labor movement, including the Central Labor Council, the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, and the New York Taxi Workers Alliance. On October 22, hundreds of Amazon workers and Teamsters rallied outside city hall, joined by representatives of other unions, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Teamsters President Sean O’Brien. O’Brien accused Menin of failing to keep her promise to bring the bill to a vote. “Keep your promises; don’t fall in love with corporate America,” O’Brien said. “Speaker Menin, you need to do what the people want — the people that put you where you’re at.” The campaign has extended well beyond the rally, with New York City Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) playing a central role alongside Teamsters Local 804. NYC-DSA has put its electoral canvassing operation to work on the bill, organizing phone banks and sending volunteers door-to-door. By October, they had knocked on more than 11,000 doors and helped bring three councilmembers on as sponsors. In Menin’s Upper East Side district alone, more than 100 volunteers knocked on 2,500 doors in a single day. Mamdani has continued campaigning for the legislation, too. At the October rally, he pointed to the contradiction at the center of Amazon’s employment arrangements. “When a driver wears an Amazon vest, drives an Amazon van, [and] follows a route Amazon set and Amazon insists that driver does not work for them, what is that if not exploitation?” he said. When reporters asked Mamdani about the possibility of dropping the ban on subcontracting and passing a narrower bill, he rejected the idea. “I don’t think that we need to have a conversation about a new bill,” he said. “I think we have all of the answers in the bill as it currently stands.” When I spoke with Julie Su, Mamdani’s deputy mayor for economic justice and the former acting US secretary of labor, about the bill earlier this year, she described Amazon’s arrangement as “a business model built on getting all the benefits of labor while disclaiming any responsibility for it.” “It is an end run around a century of labor protections that have been fought for and won,” she said. Su also took issue with Amazon’s warnings that the bill would cost workers their jobs. “It is an age-old argument by corporations who have profited massively off the backs of exploited workers, to say that working people only have two choices: a really bad job in which you’re struggling to get by, or no job at all,” she told me. “We reject that as a false choice.” Amazon has itself put drivers out of work by cutting ties with DSPs whose employees unionized. Last year in Queens, 105 drivers at Cornucopia Logistics lost their jobs when Amazon canceled its contract with the company. The drivers had organized with the Teamsters and accused Amazon of retaliating against them. Amazon denied it. In Palmdale, California, Amazon cut ties with Battle-Tested Strategies, a contractor whose eighty-four drivers had organized with the Teamsters in 2023. The NLRB later accused Amazon of illegally ending the contract and refusing to bargain. Drivers at another Amazon contractor in Skokie, Illinois, struck in 2024, alleging retaliation for organizing. Amazon denied retaliating against union supporters. The DSP arrangement has also cost New York workers jobs when union organizing wasn’t involved. Last week, the company terminated its relationship with Kaizen Management Solutions, a Manhattan contractor whose employees deliver Amazon packages on electric cargo bikes. Roughly two hundred workers learned that their employment would end November 18. Amazon said it had discovered safety violations and fraud involving the recording of drivers’ hours; some workers disputed that explanation. “This DSP model is about Amazon’s bottom line,” one worker told Streetsblog . “The model that allegedly creates jobs just laid off 200 people right before the holidays.” “I wish I could tell you I have another thing lined up but I don’t,” he added. “They didn’t even give me a month to figure it out.” Rosario met Kaizen’s owner, Ezra Tilaye, at a Teamsters picket outside the Delancey Street facility earlier this week. Tilaye, who is from Guyana, seemed as blindsided by Amazon’s decision as the workers. One driver Rosario spoke with had been on the job for only three days; another had just been promoted to dispatcher. Rosario took that as evidence that Tilaye hadn’t known the contract was about to be terminated. For Rosario, the layoffs made a mockery of Amazon’s campaign to defend small businesses, particularly those owned by minorities. “Are you protecting small businesses, or do you just not care and are pretending otherwise?” he asked. Menin called the layoffs “terrible” and said that the city would regulate Amazon “in a very significant way.” Amazon may not need to defeat the bill outright. The majority of councilmembers have signed on, but negotiations could still strip out the requirement that Amazon employ its drivers directly. Similar legislation has already been introduced in Chicago , and worker advocates want to pursue it in other cities. What survives the negotiations in New York could shape those efforts elsewhere. articles.title: 2026 Los Angeles Midterms: How Grassroots Organizing Powered Progressive Wins
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Before Dick Price and I started LA Progressive, I went to the county registrar to look up election returns for our congressional district. I think I was planning to write something for our Democratic club. What I remember clearly is how saddened I was by how few people had voted. Nearly two decades later, I sat down with Hans Johnson of the East Area Progressive Democrats to talk about a very different election. I was still taking in the news from Mississippi , where Scott Colom had become the first Black person elected to represent the state in the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction. Here in Los Angeles County , the latest count put turnout at 53.84 percent as of November 17, up from 43.65 percent in the 2022 midterm. The county had already counted more than 3.18 million ballots. I wanted to know what had changed here at home and what we could do with the opportunity voters had given us. Hans Johnson on Progressive L.A. Candidates (26:51) What it took to get voters to the polls Johnson called it a “bright blue wave of turnout.” He saw the No Kings protests as an early sign of how many people were ready to push back against the Trump administration. He also pointed to work closer to home that gets considerably less attention. Volunteers wrote postcards, neighbors met candidates, and voters got information from people they already knew and trusted. Johnson counted five victories in races his club had made priorities in November. Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass for mayor, Marissa Roy won the city attorney’s race, Sara Hernandez won the 26th State Senate District, and Angela Gonzales-Torres unseated Rep. Jimmy Gomez in the 34th Congressional District. In the statewide race for superintendent of public instruction, Richard Barrera won after campaigning against what he called the “cage of austerity” in public education. Barri Worth Girvan’s City Council victory in the West Valley also prompted Johnson to reflect on the years of organizing it took to open up a council long dominated by men. I’m a member of the East Area Progressive Democrats, and when I make it to a meeting, I’m struck by how much people know about what’s happening in their own communities. I asked Hans how he keeps up. His answer was simple. He listens. Members bring reports on transit, public education and gun violence prevention. They ask questions and share articles so people can read up on an issue and decide whether to raise it with the officials who have the power to act. LAist included the club’s ballot guide in its roundup this fall. The meetings gave me a sense of how much work goes into earning the trust that makes people reach for a guide in the first place. What happens after the votes are counted I’d seen anti-gondola signs in my neighborhood, so I asked Hans what was behind them. The proposed aerial gondola would connect Union Station to Dodger Stadium, with a stop at Los Angeles State Historic Park near Chinatown. The project’s backers present it as a zero-emission way to get to the stadium. Johnson said the club opposes it because of its potential impact on public parkland and his concern about whether the public could end up paying for it. On December 2, the California State Park and Recreation Commission is scheduled to consider an amendment to the park’s general plan for the project. The election is over, and decisions about who gets to use public land and for what purpose are already on the calendar. The same question about what follows an election applies to the people we’ve just elected. In the county’s November 17 count, Gonzales-Torres was ahead of Gomez by more than 24 percentage points. Johnson remembered her high school teachers getting involved in the campaign and club volunteers helping to write thousands of postcards. He was especially moved to hear her talk about deported veterans as the daughter of one herself. She’ll be my representative, too. I want her to succeed, and I want us to pay attention to the rules and institutions that can keep even good candidates from delivering on the promises that got them elected. On November 18, Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres voted against nominating Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker in a secret ballot of House Democrats. Jeffries won the nomination 251–11, with two Democrats casting no ballot. The full House will elect the speaker in January. Gonzales-Torres was one of eight incoming members who publicly confirmed voting against Jeffries. The other seven were Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Don Leonard of Ohio, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. Three of the 11 votes against Jeffries were still publicly unconfirmed when Axios reported the tally. Texas Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III signed the statement opposing Jeffries, but his spokesperson said he missed the vote. He was one of the two who did not cast a ballot. I’m still in wait-and-see mode about the progressive chops of the people we just elected. Gonzales-Torres was willing to break with most of her caucus on this vote. I’ll be watching how she votes on legislation and what she does when party leaders resist the policies she campaigned on. Johnson made a similar point about Sheriff Robert Luna, who had roughly 70 percent of the vote in his rematch with Alex Villanueva. Johnson welcomed the result and said the department still needs stronger civilian oversight and more transparency. Johnson said his club organized six No Kings rallies, primarily in Glendale. He wants those gatherings to continue. The people who came out to challenge Trump, he argued, can also keep the pressure on the people they helped elect. I’m still on a bit of a high from this election. I also remember walking out of the registrar’s office years ago wondering what it would take to get more of us involved. This November, hundreds of thousands more people in Los Angeles County voted than in the last midterm. I want us to bring some of that same energy to the places where decisions get made between elections. That’s where we’ll find out how much we changed.

articles.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal: A Gift to China Hawks and AI Giants
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Often, when people cheat on their spouses, they get kicked out of the house and strain their families. Not many can say they wiped out $1.8 trillion worth of share value and made the economy wobble. Yet this is exactly the case with ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang and the scandal surrounding his various infidelities, including to a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy. (Or is she?) The uncertainty around that question is part of the general murkiness of this entire affair (no pun intended), one tied into a knot of three separate political threads: the economy’s outsize reliance on the artificial intelligence industry, ruthless corporate anti-competition, and the simmering new Cold War with China. While Huang had a number of infidelities, it’s his affair with business executive Alice Huang that is central to both the global attention this has drawn and to his ouster from the company he had founded over a Denny’s meal with only $40,000 of capital, thanks to his paramour’s alleged role as a spy for the Ministry of State Security, roughly China’s equivalent to the Central Intelligence Agency. Even as the infractions piled up, it’s hard to imagine Huang — a widely admired , politically connected CEO who commanded intense loyalty from his employees — being pushed out of his own company over infidelity if not for the possibility, leaked to the press, that he fell for a Chinese government honey trap. So it’s notable that no one seems to really know whether or not Alice Huang truly was a spy. CNN reports that US intelligence agencies aren’t actually sure, with some officials viewing media reports alleging that she is as overstating the reality. At the same time, Donald Trump , Vice President J. D. Vance , and Attorney General Todd Blanche have all publicly claimed uncertainty about this central allegation. The Singaporean government went out of its way to explicitly deny The Wall Street Journal’s reporting that its officials had been concerned about her alleged spying for Beijing and investigated it. Most explosively, T he Washington Post reported that the spy claim came from one official in particular: China hawk Marco Rubio, who personally reshaped the CIA’s more ambiguous intelligence into a memo forcefully making the spy allegation and circulated it around the administration all the way back in May, to little effect. Let’s take a moment now to note how odd it is that the details of that memo then somehow made their way to the press. Let’s also take a moment to note how odd it is that neither this administration, which has zealously investigated and thrown the book at leakers, nor Rubio, who has called leakers “criminals” and once tried to throw some in prison for a decade, seem to particularly care about this leak. A Win for Hawks So what exactly is going on here? It’s too early to say for sure. But one thing we can say with certainty is that Huang was long given the side-eye by Washington’s China hawks owing to his unabashed advocacy for doing business with China, his closeness with the president, and the fact that he had used that closeness to get Trump to let Nvidia skirt US export controls and sell its chips to China. For those hawks, who Huang publicly lambasted as carrying a “badge of shame,” this was a grave offense and a threat to national security, with the possibility that China could use the advanced chips to win the “AI race” that this crowd is obsessed with. Another certainty is that these same hawks have wasted no time in seizing on the affair to push for harder-line policies against China, at a time when Trump had been edging toward a more conciliatory posture with the country, drawing growing pushback from Washington. The Trump administration has now tightened export controls on AI chips in the wake of this scandal, and a consensus is now e merging in Congress to go beyond this. China hawks are making a renewed push to tighten them even further, with parts of a fourth bill doing so now set to be added to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for 2027. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, reportedly the main figure within the administration resisting a crackdown on the export of Nvidia chips, is being publicly undermined by one of his own fellow cabinet members, facing the possibility of being investigated , and may see his head roll over the episode, all as lawmakers demand he clamp down on the chip exports. China hawks “are thrilled right now” and are “gonna win the day,” one Trump official told T he Washington Sun , while an economist who backs the stricter controls told the outlet that with Lutnick and Nvidia “sidelined, the center of gravity has shifted to Rubio-world,” since they “were the main opposition to any sort of export controls.” A Win for AI Monopolists China hawks aren’t the only ones who stand to benefit from Huang’s ouster. The battle over China’s access to high-end AI chips is, in part, a proxy for a whole other battle being fought within the industry. The removal of Huang is viewed as a blow to the movement behind open-source AI models — those that the general public can download and tinker with, as opposed to closed-source models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, where the developer has exclusive control but chooses to make the model available for public use. Open-source models also happen to be mostly the kind developed by Chinese companies, whose cheaper models US companies are increasingly turning to . Huang also happened to be a major champion for — and, more importantly, financial backer of — such models, probably because the proliferation of more AI models also means more business for Nvidia. One venture capitalist who invested in some of the same start-ups as Nvidia told the Financial Times that Huang getting the boot means “we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers.” That put him at odds with companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, whose commercial interest lies in trying to dominate the AI market and preventing the spread of open-source models that would make people less reliant on their products. Anthropic has long been an outspoken proponent of the export controls on AI chips that Huang chafed against, breaking from other industry players over the issue by backing the three restrictionist bills included in the NDAA for 2027. OpenAI, meanwhile, pulled back on its advocacy for export controls, both as Huang’s dealmaking saw it become more financially intertwined with Nvidia and to align more closely with Trump as he came under Huang’s influence, costing China hawks what they had counted as an important industry ally. But Huang’s ouster has “loosened them up a bit,” a source told Politico , with OpenAI now back to arguing in favor of those same three export control bills in the defense authorization bill for next year. In fact, it goes much further than this. Because filings show that both of these closed-source firms have thrown a small mountain of money into lobbying various arms of the federal government on this issue, including the very two organs — the State Department and the National Security Council (NSC) — that happen to be headed by Marco Rubio, China-hawk-in-chief and the main figure responsible for the spy claims about Huang’s mistress. Starting from the third quarter of this year, dating from July to the end of September — the period that came after Rubio reportedly circulated his spy allegation memo in May — OpenAI spent a whopping $1.5 million lobbying on issues that included “foreign AI capabilities and national-security risks,” lining up with Politico’s reporting that the firm had started voicing its support for export controls to Congress in recent months. This was a notable shift from 2025: that year, OpenAI’s in-house lobbying outfit had spent substantially less than this amount per quarter and hadn’t lobbied the State Department, nor does that phrase appear as a lobbying issue in that year’s filings. In other words, it’s not just that OpenAI started pushing for restricting the export of chips right after Rubio circulated his questionable memo linking Nvidia’s CEO to Chinese spying, and that it was that CEO’s removal that had “loosened them up” to do it. They also lobbied Rubio’s own department, and did it just months before that memo mysteriously leaked to the press, forcing his ouster. There is a similar pattern with the other closed-source AI giant, Anthropic, which, in that same July-to-September period paid several Trumpworld lobbying firms to work on this matter. One was Navigators Global, which that very same quarter started lobbying Congress on behalf of the AI firm on the export control provisions in the NDAA. Navigators Global’s cofounder happened to be Rubio’s very first chief of staff when he was a senator, while one of the lobbyists who worked on this issue is Andy Keiser, who for fourteen years served in various roles for ex-congressman Mike Rogers, the Trump ally who ran for Michigan’s Senate seat this year and in 2024. Sit for a moment with the fact that Anthropic was pushing this issue using a lobbying firm closely connected to the very figure arguably most responsible for driving Huang’s ouster. It’s a similar case with Ballard Partners, founded by a longtime Florida lobbyist who counts Rubio as a friend and where Trump’s recently ousted chief of staff Susie Wiles was managing partner for years before joining up with Trump in 2019 — a firm so connected that one departed Trump official has charged it “controlled” White House policy. In the third quarter, it started lobbying for Anthropic on “advocacy regarding US policy regarding AI” to the tune of $380,000, including at Rubio’s NSC, for which it employed two recently departed Trump national security personnel, one of whom had just worked at Rubio’s State Department. Another specifically Rubio-connected lobbying firm used by Anthropic for this was Continental Strategy, one of whose managing partners is Alberto Martinez — a “trusted advisor” to Rubio who worked in various roles for the former senator over the course of a decade, including chief of staff and senior strategist on his first Senate race — and which promoted Wiles’s daughter a day after Trump hired her. Martinez was among the lobbyists Continental used to lobby agencies that included Rubio’s NSC (from April to the end of June) and then Rubio’s State Department (in this just-passed third quarter) on “AI development and national security,” for which it was paid a total of $300,000 by Anthropic for these periods. Both Ballard and Continental’s roles were first reported by ZeroHedge , but this is based on my own separate analysis of Anthropic’s 2026 lobbying disclosures. It’s remarkable that at the same time the interests of Rubio-led China hawks and firms like Anthropic were crossing over, the company was literally employing Rubio’s own former loyalists to lobby the government bodies he was in charge of. This is on top of the $230,000 that Anthropic paid over the past year’s three quarters to Fierce Government Relations — a firm with a couple of Trump-connected employees — to lobby Congress and the Office of the President on export controls and the NDAA bills; another $180,000 over the same period to Aquia for the same issues; $60,000 to the Democratic firm Avenue Solutions to lobby Congress on the NDAA starting in the third quarter; and the nearly $6 million it spent in-house in that period to lobby on issues that included these topics. In that last case, it used a longtime staffer of Sen. Patty Murray, who had been demanding in recent months that Trump impose these stricter export controls. So in summary, the two closed-source AI firms that view China’s AI industry as a threat to their own bottom line have done the following: lobbied heavily for these China-squeezing export controls this year; appear to have in some cases ramped up their lobbying on this after Rubio circulated the sensational but unproven claim that led to Huang’s booting; hired former staffers from Trumpworld to do that lobbying; and in particular, hired lobbying firms and used lobbyists with long-standing connections to Rubio specifically to do it. The picture that emerges is of the unmistakable — some might say convenient — convergence of interests between Washington’s China hawks and AI giants, and the downright eerie overlap between the offices and personnel of what are in theory meant to be two different entities. Even more convenient, all of this has come to a head just as one of these AI giants, Anthropic, was set to embark on its initial public offering, which it did yesterday, raising $81 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record. Like I said: convenient. A Bet Without Consent Less convenient is another thing we can say for sure, which is that, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO aside, this entire saga is causing heart rates to spike. That’s because Nvidia — and, owing to his domination of the company and personal role in every deal it struck, Huang himself — is a load-bearing force for an industry straining to stay standing up, passing out the necessary capital for flagship AI firms, start-ups, the building of data centers, and the neo-cloud firms that provide the computing power for firms that can’t build their own. In fact, Nvidia effectively came to the rescue of one of those neo-clouds, CoreWeave, when its bonds recently entered distressed territory after skeptical investors started dumping the company’s debt en masse. Huang’s ouster throws the industry into uncertainty as it waits to see, first, if any one person is able to actually fill Huang’s shoes, and second, if the person who does has the same kind of appetite for risk that he did. So far, indications are that the interim CEO does not , and with the firm about to be dragged through an acre of thorns in the form of congressional hearings and other scrutiny, it would not be surprising if it embarks on a more conservative approach going forward. That doesn’t necessarily mean that the AI industry is headed toward an imminent crash. But this is all spectacularly bad timing given the spate of setbacks and growing investor doubts it’s been weathering, the last one being an incoming US Congress dominated by politicians who ran and won on restricting the data centers that AI firms need to keep being built to stay financially viable. At this point, you might stop to marvel at the absurdity that — because of the way we’ve structured our economy, the way it’s intertwined with US foreign policy, and the corrupting distortion of the Washington revolving door and influence-peddling — one man’s horniness threatens to bring down the US economy and ramp up conflict between two nuclear-armed powers. It’s just one of several layers of absurdity to a situation and industry that, without ever being consulted on it, we have all as a society been roped into staking our collective future on. Huang is not the first or last CEO who will have a personal scandal that can be exploited by shadowy forces with their own ulterior motives. But because of the nature of the AI industry, whichever executive draws embarrassing headlines next, it’s gossip that we’re all going to have to care deeply about. articles.title: Billionaires Always Want to Maintain Control
articles.author: Sophie Bandarkar
articles.content: In October, Meta released a filing saying that Mark Zuckerberg had threatened to leave California in anticipation of Proposition 40 , the billionaire wealth tax on the 2026 state ballot, which was defeated 53 to 47 percent. According to the document, Zuckerberg told the board he was “evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California,” and that any steps toward doing so, including listing his residential real estate on the market, “would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees.” In response, the board quickly mobilized to negotiate a deal: Meta agreed to issue a new class of nonvoting (“Class C”) stock, which will be distributed to all shareholders in January 2027. This would have allowed Zuckerberg to sell his shares to convert a portion of his wealth into the billions in cash he would need to meet his potential tax liability, without losing his near-supermajority voting share. In exchange, he agreed to stay in the state for at least eight years and keep his $1 annual salary. Conveniently, the new stock will also allow Meta to raise capital for artificial intelligence investments without changing the decision-making composition of the company. In the fallout of the proposition’s defeat, it’s useful to reflect on what the Meta deal can help us understand for the long-term movement to tax the ultrarich’s wealth. What Proposition 40 Was Prop 40 was designed as a onetime 5 percent tax, payable over five years, on the net worth of California residents with over $1 billion who lived in the state as of January 1, 2026. The proposition was written by legal and economics faculty and introduced by the health care workers’ union Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers (SEIU-UHW). The goal of the tax was to raise around $100 billion, which would offset roughly 90 percent of the federal budget cuts to health programs, including Medi-Cal, since the beginning of the second Trump administration — and in particular, since the passing of the 2025 “Big Beautiful Bill,” which takes effect this January. According to research by economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, California’s billionaire wealth reached around $2.3 trillion by mid-2026, which is roughly equal to the total income reported by every Californian in a year. This wealth is both extremely concentrated and recent: it’s increased by 144 percent in just three years. The approximately 250 billionaires who would qualify only pay about 0.2 percent of their wealth in California income tax each year, representing 2.4 percent of total California income tax revenue. The four richest billionaires, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang, pay only 0.07 percent of their wealth. If Proposition 40 had passed, it would have been the first tax of its kind and the culmination of decades of advocacy by policymakers and researchers across the world working to expose how dramatically economic inequality has grown and the degree of billionaires’ tax avoidance. This is particularly salient in California, the fourth-largest economy in the world and home to fifty-eight of the Fortune 500 companies. Companies in the Bay Area alone represent 35 percent of the market cap of the world’s top hundred companies. This makes the state an ideal place to experiment with taxing the ultrawealthy. Why It Failed The initiative failed for myriad, well-documented reasons. Primarily, it faced a concerted and incredibly well-funded opposition campaign. Its opponents, mostly ultrawealthy donors, spent $378.4 million against the measure (compared to the yes campaign’s budget of $33.5 million). Google cofounder and Donald Trump supporter Sergey Brin alone donated $102 million, and also funded two additional Propositions (41 and 42) designed to block the tax if it passed. California Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure and endorsed Proposition 42, stating , “Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level.” According to Rigel Robinson, former Berkeley city councilmember and Democratic public policy consultant, It would be a mistake to see the electoral outcome of Proposition 40 as a clear rejection of its goal from voters. There was the enormous and well-funded opposition campaign, and competing and confusing ballot measures designed to nullify the measure. Proposition 42, which was put on the ballot to prevent Proposition 40 (and future versions of it) from taking effect even if it did pass, was sold to voters as a protection for retirement savings. However, in California and across the country, candidates won on a message of seizing power from billionaires and championing affordability. In many ways, this is the sort of message Bernie Sanders tried to bring to the Democratic agenda a decade ago. Voters across the country have demonstrated that redistribution and economic justice are clear priorities, and we cannot let the outcome of this proposition diminish the ground won. There were also concerns about the legality and mechanics of the legislation — in particular, that it was introduced as a onetime proposition, was not national, and was technically a retroactive tax, since it applied to anyone living in the state as of January 2026. And as Fred Glass explained in Jacobin , California’s labor and progressive forces were unable to form a unified front in support of the measure. While disappointing, it’s helpful to historicize the initiative and the broader movement to tax the assets of the ultrawealthy alongside other fights for redistribution. The federal income tax, for example, took several attempts before successfully passing. It took the Sixteenth Amendment passing in 1913 to make it permanent. SEIU-UHW has already said it plans to try again in 2028, and Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna have introduced a bill at the federal level this spring. Billionaire Wealth Is Money Today From the Meta deal, we can learn two things. First, it is possible for tech leadership to convert their wealth into liquidity. One of the most persistent arguments against taxing the ultrawealthy is that their money isn’t “real,” since it’s mostly in shares of companies whose value rises and falls with the market. Because of this, it shouldn’t be treated as income. Stocks are legal claims on future production whose prices are set by expected returns. It is not uncommon for the companies who issue them to have not yet produced anything profitable or concrete. SpaceX’s shares were the most valuable in history at the time of their initial public offering (IPO), even though its AI division had lost $2 for every dollar of revenue it earned in 2025. In other words, a stock is a title of ownership to a slice of the surplus value a company will produce. In the Marxian sense , this is an example of fictitious capital and inherently speculative. However, “speculative” does not mean unreal. As Dimitris P. Sotiropoulos, John Milios, and Spyros Lapatsioras write in A Political Economy of Contemporary Capitalism and its Crisis: Demystifying Finance , fictitious capital is not detached from real production but a necessary phase within its totality, and claims on future income can become commodities in their own right. These can be traded, priced, and converted into money at any time. A stock is not just a promise of future wealth; it is wealth (and command over the labor of others) today. Modern finance for the AI sector also has a remarkable capacity to innovate and reinvent itself, and the financial engineering to create the Class C share is another demonstration of the sector’s remarkable capacity to adapt to secure endless capital for the AI rush. Another Front of Contestation Second, tech executives are most concerned with losing control of their companies. As economist and tax expert Gabriel Zucman told me, “the existence of super-voting shares and the Zuckerberg and Proposition 40 episode more generally highlight that what matters most to billionaires, even more than their wealth, is their power to exert control over the giant businesses they own. This is indeed their greatest power.” He also commented on X that the opposition to the wealth tax could not be driven by concerns about losing money, since the onetime 5 percent liability would “merely bring billionaire’s fortunes back to where they stood a few weeks ago, at the beginning of September.” Meta is not an isolated case, and a dual-class share system (which allows companies to sell shares to the public, while a small group keeps most of the votes) has been on the rise. When SpaceX went public, Elon Musk floated only 3–4 percent of the company and retained 42 percent of its shares, but 85 percent of its voting share through his “super-voting stock.” Anthropic’s IPO includes five types of stock, which specifically gives the cofounders the ability to keep a say over the controlling vote even if they give away 98 percent of their shares. The most valuable companies in the world are increasingly owned by a handful of individuals insulated from markets, shareholders, and other public mechanisms of accountability. As Fred Glass wrote , Proposition 40 is a lost battle, not a lost war. Amid the manufactured panic over the tax, Zuckerberg seized the political moment to negotiate a deal with his company. The outcome of their agreement deepens our understanding of how to anticipate and oppose the coordinated class response against taxing extreme wealth. First, the shares of future value held by tech billionaires are not just abstractions but real money today, necessary to the current cycle of reproduction. And second, billionaires will fight hardest to protect not their fortune but their control. The Left’s political project has to include a new front of contestation beyond fighting for shares of the returns tech companies produce. Countering the enclosure of the AI economy will require reclaiming democratic control over the infrastructures of this intelligence in the first place. articles.content: Enjoy your November National Political Committee (NPC) newsletter! Our NPC is an elected 27-person body (including both YDSA Co-Chairs) which functions as the board of directors of DSA. This month, check out electoral wins, take a labor solidarity pledge, find out more about our arms embargo campaign, and more! And to make sure you get our newsletters in your inbox, sign up here! From the National Political Committee — Cool Weather, Hot DSA Wins As the weather cools down, DSA organizing is heating up! Our wave of electoral wins earlier this month shows that our ideas are popular and practical, and that DSA members are putting in the work to make real, lasting change where we live and across the country. More than 120 DSA nationally and locally endorsed candidates won their elections. And chapters ran dozens of successful ballot campaigns to tax the rich, protect trans kids, stand up for housing justice, and more! More than 1000 people joined our post-election call — more on that from Southern electeds, Teamsters organizer Tony Rosario, and Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter leaders here! Our endorsed candidates included labor organizers, teachers, healthcare workers, and more. They’ve already been fighting to end the genocide in Palestine, tax billionaires, protect our communities from ICE, and more. Once in office, they’ll continue to speak out for working class people and help build a movement for the many, not the money. Recently, we had the chance to speak to Richard D. Wolff, professor of economics and co-founder of Democracy at Work. During our discussion, Professor Wolff said that he’d spoken with his neighbors about Zohran Mamdani. Even the ones less engaged with politics knew that a politician willing to call themselves a socialist was different from Republicans and establishment Democrats — and they wanted that difference! Leaning forward, Professor Wolff spoke directly to us, and to DSA members like you across the country. “You underestimate how powerful you are, because of the moment in which you exist… The organization you’re building — crucial… It’s for you, the future. And if you go for it, you can get it.” You can see the whole video here. Professor Wolff is right, and working class people know it. That’s why DSA joins increased over 650% after Election Day! DSA chapters and members are heating things up, and YOU have the power to come together for a brighter future. Attend the December Leadership Intensive Saturday 12/12 – Sunday 12/13. RSVP today! articles.title: Nolan Well
articles.author: Melina Abdullah
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me to be a Christian? Acts 26:28 Christian Anthony Claudio is a righteous young Black man of conscience from upstate New York. He is a central fixture in his family and tightly-knit community, where he works with special needs children and can be relied on to help friends when their cars break down. At just 25-years-old, he owns his own home, pays his own bills, has never been arrested, and stands as a model of what it means to be a good brother, son, friend, and neighbor. He lives up to his name – Christian. Christian saw himself in Nolan Wells, the 18-year-old son of Christine and Elmore Wonsley, a college athlete, who loved his parents and siblings, a friend to all and an enemy of none. Nolan was killed this past July 4th in the midst of an all white “friend” group in Mississippi. When the entire Mississippi system of (in)justice refused to prosecute anyone for Nolan’s death, instead calling his death an “accidental drowning,” from 1200 miles away, Christian took what action he could. He called the court clerk in Jackson County, Mississippi and asked why. For that simple act, Christian has been charged with making terroristic threats, arrested, jailed for weeks in New York, then extradited to Jackson County, Mississippi, the same county that is covering up the murder of Nolan Wells. Related: Black Lives Matter LA Has 10 Demands for Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman There is no publicly available recording of Christian’s call. The sole public record of the alleged threat is an affidavit of Jackson County Detective Justin Quinnelly. Social media reports are swirling: that the clerk who received the call is the sheriff’s wife, that she’s friends with Judge Ashlee Cole – the stepmother of one of the white boys embroiled in the killing of Nolan Wells, that the sheriff has a long history of putting Black folks “in their place.” Christian is now the sixth person charged for asking questions about the death of Nolan Wells. Others, from Illinois and California also have pending cases. NFL star Terrell Owens is being sued for posting about the case, declaring that those involved should be arrested. You know who hasn’t been charged or suffered any negative repercussions? Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, and Morgan Seymour…the white “friends”…sons of judges and of the confederacy. They have gone on with their lives, protected by a system designed to do just that, and crowdfunded to the tune of almost a quarter million dollars. This is the devil’s work carried by Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch, who said that the investigation of Nolan’s death would be left to the local District Attorney, but any “tampering” would be handled by her office. The same Attorney General who deemed the murder of 1-year-old Baby #KohenWiley by Senatobia police “justified,” who signed off on the murder of #JaylenLewis by Mississippi Capitol police, refused charges in at least 20 more Black people killed by police, and paid restitution to the cop who killed #GeorgeRobinson. Fitch is the same Attorney General whose family is preserving the home of the first Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan on their plantation land. Fitch has announced her run for Mississippi Governor in 2028. Related: Representation Is Not Liberation: Why I Vote My Values, Not My Loyalties Fitch’s reign does not go unchallenged. Ms. Bettersten Wade, mother of #DexterWade and sister of #GeorgeRobinson – both killed by Jackson police, holds regular protests at Fitch’s office and Jackson People’s Assembly has been carrying the long and hard work for years. Black Lives Matter Youth Vanguard member, Jerome Richardson, who himself was arrested with charges pending for being present during an anti-ICE action at a church in St. Paul, Minnesota (along with journalists Georgia Fort, Don Lemon, attorney Nekima Levy-Armstrong, BLM Grassroots organizers Chauntyll Allen, Satara Strong, and 30 others), has thrown himself into the unseen work of organizing for Christian Claudio’s release. Grassroots activists from Mississippi’s gulf coast are standing strong to ensure Christian’s safe return home. Black Lives Matter Grassroots supporters have pitched in to ensure that there are funds for his bond, travel, and care. Even a Black bailbondswoman has stepped up, cutting her fees to ensure that Christian is released quickly and safely. On Tuesday, Black students at UCLA are protesting for Nolan Wells. This weekend Latinx allies are rallying in Mariachi Plaza for Nolan Wells and Baby #KohenWiley, who was killed by police outside a Walmart in Senatobia, Mississippi. On Friday, in Mississippi, Ms. Bettersten will lead another protest outside Lynn Fitch’s office. Nolan Wells’ parents have asked us to keep saying his name. We must and we will. Christian’s next courtdate is in February. Conditions of his release include an ankle monitor and no posting on social media. But they cannot quiet all of us. We must continue to fight for Nolan, for Kohen, and for all of our people…in Mississippi and everywhere. Forces of evil have arrested one, but let a million Christians be inspired to do good and righteous work. Los Angeles Sentinel

articles.title: What the Ottomans Tell Us About Plunder and Capitalism
articles.author: Y. Doğan Çetinkaya
articles.content: Vivek Chibber’s recent interview on the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism and Vijay Prashad’s response in Monthly Review have reopened fundamental questions about capitalism’s origins, colonialism, and the transition from feudalism to capitalism in world history. Drawing on my research into Ottoman history, I want to make the case that societies beyond Europe belong in this history not simply for their contributions to the rise of capitalism in the West but for their own internal transformations. The origins of capitalism and its subsequent development through colonialism are distinct historical problems. Ottoman history allows us to draw this distinction by examining a transition beyond the northwestern European cases at the center of this debate. On the central question of this debate, I am closer to Chibber: I support his distinction between the emergence of capitalism and colonial plunder, and his insistence on looking to the internal transformation of feudal society for an explanation. I also accept Robert Brenner’s account of the English transition. My disagreement concerns whether capitalist relations could also emerge from within other feudal societies, before Western economic domination and along different historical paths. I agree with some of Prashad’s criticisms of political Marxism, but that agreement does not extend to his account of capitalism’s origins. In the Ottoman Empire, too, capitalism developed out of the internal dynamics of feudal society without relying on colonial plunder, and before Western economic domination and the Industrial Revolution. This process transformed both society and the state, later laying the groundwork for internal colonization. Ottoman history thus brings into focus the distinctions between capitalism’s emergence, its colonial expansion, and the rise of the West — processes that Prashad folds into a single explanation. Wealth Is Not Capital Chibber’s starting point is that the accumulation of wealth and the emergence of capitalist social relations are distinct processes. A society that possesses vast financial resources does not necessarily organize its production along capitalist lines. Nor does the wealth that colonizers plundered create capitalism on its own. Chibber acknowledges that once capitalist relations have emerged, such wealth can accelerate their development. Supporting his argument about capitalism’s origins therefore does not require denying colonialism’s importance in its subsequent history. On the contrary, it allows us to ask within which social relations, and at what historical stage, colonialism acquired that importance. The crucial advance we need to preserve in the debate over capitalism’s origins is the shift from explaining it through the quantity of wealth to explaining it through the character of the relations of production. Here the meaning of primitive accumulation becomes clear. Before asking how enough money accumulated to finance investment, we need to explain how producers’ relationships to their means of subsistence and production changed. Capital’s power over production and labor depends on social relations that allow money to function as a social power. The emergence of those relations involves dispossession, coercion, and class struggle. But we cannot equate all these processes with colonialism. Transformations within feudal society have their own history of dispossession and struggle. To treat colonial plunder as capitalism’s necessary starting point is to subsume the very history we need to explain under a different process. The value of Chibber’s intervention lies in bringing this social transformation back to the center of the debate over capitalism’s origins. Just as trade existed before capitalism, so did plunder, invasion, and conquest. Their existence alone cannot explain the emergence of capitalist social relations. We should also note that Chibber does not locate capitalism’s early development exclusively in England. He also includes Holland and other parts of the Low Countries in his account of the transformation of northwestern Europe. I accept Brenner’s account of the emergence of capitalism in England. My objection is not to its validity for England but to ruling out the possibility that capitalist relations could also emerge from feudalism’s internal dynamics in other societies. Such transitions need not reproduce England’s historical trajectory or institutional forms. Different paths need not contradict political Marxism’s definition of capitalism: the social relations that define capitalism can emerge under different historical conditions and take different forms. This is the case I am making by bringing Ottoman history into the debate. I am not rejecting the explanation of the English transition but challenging the use of its specific forms as a yardstick that excludes other histories of capitalist development. Chibber also points to northwestern Europe’s stronger growth as one reason to locate capitalism’s early development there. Here too we need to be clear about what the evidence allows us to conclude. It is one thing to explain why certain societies grew faster by pointing to capitalist relations; it is another to claim that capitalist relations existed only in those faster-growing societies. The second proposition does not follow from the first. A society can become capitalist without becoming a leader in capitalist development. To identify capitalism, we need to establish whether capital accumulation has come to govern production and the conditions under which producers secure their livelihoods. Faster economic growth may be a consequence of capitalist relations, but it is not what defines them. Nor can we equate the development of productive forces with economic growth or its pace. It involves changes in productive capacity, including productive techniques and the organization of labor, which we cannot reduce to increases in output. Northwestern Europe’s stronger growth therefore cannot by itself establish that slower-growing societies remained feudal or exclude the possibility of capitalist transitions elsewhere. The distinction between capitalism’s emergence and economic supremacy that we defend against Prashad must also hold when we assess Chibber’s account. Origins and Expansion Here I agree with Prashad’s critique of political Marxism’s explanatory framework. We cannot confine the history of capitalism to the history of English agriculture. But moving beyond that limit requires more than bringing in societies outside Europe solely for their contributions to Europe’s capitalist development. In such an account, the rest of the world enters the explanation, but the transformation it sets out to explain remains Europe’s. Changes in those societies’ own relations of production disappear. Overcoming Eurocentrism requires more than adding examples of what the rest of the world supplied to the West. We must also investigate the emergence of capitalism within these societies’ own histories. Prashad does of course discuss the transformation of labor and social reproduction in colonized societies, so I am not reducing his account to a tally of the wealth that colonizers transferred to Europe. My objection is to making colonial connections the overarching framework for explaining the emergence of capitalism. Explaining transformations under colonial domination does not also explain transitions in which domination played no constitutive role. Colonial relations cannot be the only way we connect societies in a global explanation. Prashad makes clear that he does not see colonialism as mechanically producing capitalism. His argument is that we cannot understand capitalism as it historically developed — industrial, global, racialized, and imperial — apart from colonial dispossession. Nor does he discuss only accumulation after the Industrial Revolution: he also examines early plantations and transformations in colonial production. Prashad writes: “If you ignore colonialism and the machine, you do not get the genesis of industrial capitalism, only the emergence of certain social relations.” Yet the Industrial Revolution was itself a historical outcome of capitalist development, and industrial capitalism a further stage in that development. These developments transformed capitalist relations that had already emerged; they cannot serve as the defining criteria for capitalism itself. Explaining the emergence of those relations therefore addresses the question of capitalism’s origins. It is not simply an incomplete explanation of industrial capitalism. By making a later stage of capitalist development the measure of capitalism itself, Prashad shifts the question from how capitalist relations emerged to how they subsequently developed. The emergence of those social relations is itself the transformation we need to investigate. We must distinguish their subsequent combination with colonialism, or their development into a new phase through mechanized production, from the causes of their emergence. When that distinction is precisely what is at issue, substituting capitalism’s entire subsequent history for the question of its origins does not resolve the disagreement. My question for Prashad, then, goes beyond whether capitalism is conceivable without colonialism. The capitalist transformation I identify in the Ottoman Empire is not a thought experiment about what might have happened had colonialism never existed but a historical process we need to explain. Why should capitalist relations that developed without colonialism fall outside an account of “capitalism as it actually emerged”? Defining the West’s colonial and industrial development as capitalism’s real history, while excluding other paths to capitalism, does not resolve the question of origins. It narrows the history we set out to explain. The same problem arises in the relationship between primitive accumulation and colonialism. Colonial dispossession can be one means of separating producers from the means of production and accumulating capital. It does not follow that we must define primitive accumulation, as an explanation of the emergence of capitalist relations, through colonialism. We need to distinguish the establishment of capitalist relations from their subsequent expansion into new areas and their reproduction. Colonialism can play an enormous role in this second process. But projecting that role backward changes the explanation of capitalism’s origins. My objection to Prashad is not that he discusses colonial dispossession, but that he places this connection at the center of the question of origins. The social conditions under which capitalism emerged without colonialism then drop out of the explanation. We therefore cannot treat the emergence of capitalism, the West’s global dominance, and the Industrial Revolution as different names for the same problem. The first asks how new relations of production emerged; the second, how the West established its dominance on a world scale; the third, how the technical and social organization of production changed radically. These processes shape one another, but an explanation of one cannot substitute for an explanation of another. Colonialism’s importance to the West’s rise or industrialization does not establish that capitalism originated in colonialism. We are challenging the use of later developments as founding causes of relations that had already emerged. The early appearance of colonial practices does not establish this causal link either. The fact that two processes unfolded at the same time does not show that one produced the other. Establishing that requires us to identify the mechanisms through which colonial appropriation brought capitalist relations of production into being. The strength of the Ottoman case lies in shifting the debate from a hypothetical world without colonialism to the question of how these relations actually emerged. The Ottoman Transition My argument is that capitalist relations in the Ottoman Empire emerged from within feudal society between roughly 1550 and 1650. After 1650, these relations reinforced one another and became increasingly decisive in shaping social reproduction. This chronology rules out explaining the origins of Ottoman capitalism as a consequence of the West’s later economic domination. It also prevents us from treating the absence of large-scale mechanized industry as proof of capitalism’s absence. What we need to investigate is the transformation of Ottoman society from within during this period. In this light, we see not a feudal society standing still in the face of a capitalist West but a history in which productive forces developed, relations of production changed, and a new social structure took shape through class struggle. Recent contributions to Ottoman economic and social history include Mehmet Kuru ’s work on Izmir’s regional economy, Mehmet Ali Çelik ’s research on çiftliks and agrarian labor, and Önder Eren Akgül ’s study of capital accumulation and dispossession in western Anatolia. These studies help illuminate changes in Ottoman production, property, and class relations across different periods. What drives this transformation is not the first appearance of trade or money, both of which already existed in feudal society. What changes is the relationship between the conditions that allow producers to continue producing and control over the surplus. When merchant capital begins to organize production through credit, the supply of raw materials, and control over output, the movement of capital comes to govern the continuity of production. Producers’ relationship to the market can shift from merely selling what they have left over to depending on it to sustain their livelihoods and production. The interpretation I am developing in ongoing research concerns how changes in property, credit, and labor relations increasingly placed the continuation of production under capital’s control. Demonstrating this requires more than evidence of expanding trade or growing indebtedness: it requires tracing how class struggle transformed producers’ access to the means of production and subsistence. Competitive pressure is one mechanism to investigate within this process, but we cannot reduce the transformation to producers losing their holdings because they could not compete. It is in this transformation that I look for the emergence of Ottoman capitalism. The starting point of this explanation is not wealth that colonial plunder brought in from outside but changes within existing social relations. Those changes concern not only who controls the surplus but also how it flows back into reproduction. As the expansion of production, control over labor, and access to markets intertwine, accumulation begins to determine the conditions of social reproduction. Capital thus confronts producers not simply as a power that buys their output but as a social relation that governs the conditions under which production can continue. The existence of trade does not prove the existence of capitalism. But it does not follow that merchant capital cannot reorganize production or help transform feudal class relations. An increase in the volume of trade is not the same as the subordination of production to capital. This is not a story of capitalism emerging spontaneously from the continuous expansion of markets but a history of qualitative change in capital’s relationship to production. The development of productive forces is also part of this transformation. A deeper division of labor, a larger scale of production, connections between different branches of production, and the reorganization of labor all increase society’s productive power even before mechanization. This development proceeds alongside changes in relations of production and struggles over control of the surplus. The conflicting interests of peasants, artisans, merchants, local ruling elites, and the state shape the direction and form of the transformation. To speak of feudalism’s internal dynamics is not to tell a story of technological progress unfolding on its own. It is to understand capitalism’s emergence as a history in which productive forces and relations of production develop and reshape one another through class struggle. Producers’ efforts to preserve their access to land and means of subsistence come up against the ruling classes’ attempts to extract a larger surplus. The terms of debt, taxation, and control over production take shape through these conflicts. The outcome of the transition is not a destination that feudal society contained from the outset, but the historical product of struggles to preserve and transform existing relations. The development of productive forces, then, is neither an engine operating independently of class relations nor an outcome that appears only after capitalism has emerged, but part of the social process that explains the transition itself. The Ottoman Empire’s fiscal transformation is part of this same history. Three changes increasingly tied control over the surplus to relations of capital and credit. The tımar system (rights the state granted to collect agrarian revenues, often in return for military service) changed, tax farming ( iltizam ) expanded, and the state later introduced lifetime tax farms ( malikâne ). None of these institutions, taken on its own, proves the existence of capitalism. But when we examine them alongside changes in production, property, market dependence, and accumulation, they show that the state itself was changing within the same social process. This moves us away from viewing capitalism as a sphere that emerges within society after the state retreats, as much of the literature assumes. The struggles that reorganize relations between producers and those who appropriate the surplus also transform the state’s sources of revenue and its social foundations. This history does not require the Ottoman Empire to replicate the institutions of the English transition. When we turn England’s specific forms of property and labor into universal criteria for capitalism, we fail to recognize capital’s command over production in other societies. Treating the transition from feudalism to capitalism as a problem of world history does not mean equating capitalism with trade wherever it occurs. To speak of a transition to the same mode of production is not to insist that every society follow the same historical path. This distinction also challenges the assumption that, once capitalism had emerged, it could take root in other societies only through external diffusion. Of course, speaking of the Ottoman Empire’s internal dynamics does not mean treating it as a society isolated from the world. Trade, war, and flows of money are part of this history. But the existence of external connections does not show that the West introduced capitalism or that colonial plunder gave birth to it. What we need to explain are the social relations within which those connections operated. Placing the Ottoman capitalist transformation before the West’s decisive economic influence does not write the outside world out of the story; it changes the direction of causality. The West’s later influence acted on capitalist relations that had already begun to emerge. Nor does their subsequent development under conditions of external dependence prove that their origins lay elsewhere. Dependency cannot substitute for an explanation of origins. For the same reason, late industrialization is a separate issue. If we measure the existence of capitalism by the prevalence of mechanized production, we end up defining Ottoman relations of production in terms of a technological gap with the West. Yet capitalist societies do not develop at the same pace, occupy the same international position, or enjoy the same opportunities for accumulation. Colonialism can play a decisive role in widening these inequalities and securing the supremacy of particular capitalist states. Here we move from the question of origins to that of uneven capitalist development, where the colonial accumulation and industrial transformation that Prashad emphasizes acquire explanatory force. But this explanation does not erase histories in which capitalist relations emerged earlier and without colonial plunder. Accepting Prashad’s emphasis on colonialism does not require abandoning Chibber’s distinction concerning capitalism’s origins. The fact that Ottoman capitalism did not originate in colonial plunder does not mean that the empire stood outside later wars and struggles over the division of the world. Its participation in those struggles and wars as a capitalist state does not show that it owed its transition to capitalism to resources it extracted from colonies abroad. We need to distinguish the state’s later political position from the origins of society’s capitalist transformation. The same distinction applies to the empire’s long history of conquest. Earlier conquests and relations of taxation do not prove that capitalism emerged from colonial plunder. Empire and capitalist colonialism are not the same historical category. We must reassess the relationship between them as relations of production and the social character of the state change. From Capitalist Transformation to Internal Colonization The transformation of the Ottoman state into a capitalist state is therefore the next step in the argument. Capitalism does more than create new sources of profit for particular sections of society. Through control over property, labor, and the surplus, it also changes how the state reproduces itself. What makes a state capitalist is not that its rulers become merchants or that it builds factories but that social relations become organized around the requirements of capital accumulation, with class struggles unfolding on that basis. Capitalist relations emerging from within Ottoman society deepen alongside the state’s fiscal and administrative transformation. The form of state that emerges from this transformation also begins to view the empire’s vast domains in a new light and to reorganize them accordingly. It is in the wake of this transformation that I situate internal colonization — the process I call self-colonialism . The Ottoman Empire did not owe its transition to capitalism to the plunder of colonies abroad; as the state became capitalist, it already ruled vast territories and diverse communities toward which it could direct its colonial practices. Its territories in the Balkans, the Middle East, Anatolia, the Caucasus, and North Africa became the terrain on which it established new internal relations of domination. Holding these territories is not the same as reorganizing them as internal colonies, which involved a capitalist state transforming earlier imperial rule to serve new purposes within a new set of social relations. In this transformation, the state ties civilizing rhetoric to remaking peripheral communities into populations it can govern and tax and whose labor can be controlled. Scholars have explored Ottoman colonialism from different perspectives: Nilay Özok-Gündoğa through resource extraction in Kurdistan, İlkay Yılmaz through security policies in the eastern provinces, and Ella Fratantuono through immigrant settlement. Selim Deringil and Ussama Makdisi examine the colonial outlook and civilizing claims of Ottoman elites. My question here is how these forms of domination relate to capitalism’s origins. I argue that internal colonization follows the capitalist transformation of society and the state; as it unfolds, it can intensify dispossession and open up new opportunities for accumulation. We can thus establish the causal sequence without denying the relationship between colonialism and capitalism. Internal colonization did not create Ottoman capitalism; a capitalist transformation already underway laid the social and political groundwork that made internal colonization possible. I am not proposing a single historical sequence valid for all societies, only specifying the direction of the causal relationship we need to explain in the Ottoman case. Here the question is not how colonialism created capitalism but how capitalist transformation reshaped state domination and laid the groundwork for colonial practices. This sequence does not imply that capitalism emerged without violence. The dissolution of feudal relations and the formation of capitalist relations involved conflicts over producers’ rights to their means of subsistence, their labor, and the surplus they produced. But treating every act of dispossession as colonialism prevents us from distinguishing changes in class relations from the specific history of colonial domination. We need to distinguish capitalism’s origins from colonialism not to downplay colonial violence but to explain the historical connections between different forms of domination. In the Ottoman case, this distinction allows us to trace the capitalist transformation first, then examine how it extended into internal colonization through state action. Recognizing colonialism’s immense importance to capitalist development does not require locating capitalism’s origins in it. This is the fundamental distinction on which I agree with Chibber and part ways with Prashad. In the Ottoman Empire, capitalism emerged from within feudal society and transformed both society and the state, and internal colonization followed. This history shows that accepting the analysis of the English transition does not require ruling out capitalism’s origins in other societies. Writing a world history of capitalism requires us to explain more than the world’s contributions to the making of the West. We must also explain how the world itself changed. We therefore cannot reduce the transition from feudalism to capitalism to an English or European story. Capitalism’s origins belong to a world history broader than the history of Western domination.
