articles.title: A Nobel Prize for Being Wrong
articles.author: Francesco Lamperti
articles.content: The Nobel Prize in Economics isn’t mentioned in Alfred Nobel’s will. Rather, the gong was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, which still funds it today. As Avner Offer and Gabriel Söderberg show in their book The Nobel Factor , this is no mere historical curiosity, for the prize’s origins can be understood against the backdrop of a conflict between Swedish social democracy and the champions of the market. Recognizing economists with the prestigious Nobel Prize was supposed to grant their theories the authority of the natural sciences such as physics and chemistry. Yet these imperfect theories do more than just describe the world: they help guide economic policy decisions that affect the lives of millions of people. The 2026 prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford drew this issue into especially sharp focus. According to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the two economists provided the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” developing tools capable of smoothing out the peaks and troughs of the economy. The official statement even claims that their research has made the management of major crises far more effective. The problem is that the models in question, grounded in the contributions of Hall and Woodford, have not helped stabilize economies, as the 2008 crisis clearly demonstrated. Such models have, however, convinced many economists that they could do so. Internal consistency was passed off as a real understanding of the dynamics of capitalist economies; theoretical elegance was equated with empirical validity; and apparent stability was misread as an absence of crises. Decisively, this illusion of control was not confined to academic inquiry but guided the economic policies of governments and central banks. This fueled an excessive confidence in monetary policy’s ability to stabilize both inflation and the real economy while ignoring those financial risks that would overwhelm the global economy with the subprime mortgage crisis. An Economy Tailored to the Model In the 1970s, stagflation challenged the statistical relationships through which a certain vintage of “Keynesian” macroeconomics interpreted production, unemployment, and inflation. A “New Classical Macroeconomics” offered a radical response: to study the dynamics of capitalist economies by starting with the consumption, savings, and labor choices of a single hyperrational individual capable of predicting the future based on all available information. Replacing the interactions of millions of people and firms with a single imaginary individual was a convenient shortcut to avoid seriously addressing the problems of general-equilibrium models. But this meant sweeping aside the very problems that economic science has to understand and explain: involuntary unemployment, distributional conflicts, inequality, systemic risk, and crises. This was the context in which Hall published his famous 1978 paper on consumption. If a representative household rationally chooses how much to consume in each period based on the income it expects to earn over its entire lifetime, changes in consumption head on a “random walk,” because they depend solely on new information, which is by definition unpredictable. This theoretical result implies that consumption depends solely on the income expected to be earned over a lifetime, but this contrasts with the behavior of millions of households whose consumption depends on their monthly income. In fact, as early as 1989, empirical evidence showed that the predictions from Hall’s model were incorrect, since a considerable portion of consumers made spending decisions based on current, rather than permanent, income. Subsequent research has confirmed the importance of liquidity constraints that limit consumption and differences in wealth among households. And this is no minor detail: for a low-income or indebted household, a government transfer can immediately increase consumption, just as a reduction in interest rates can. Income distribution and the composition of fiscal policies thus turn out to be decisive. But in Hall’s model, as in all models built around a mythical representative consumer, these differences are absent by design. Hall is also famous for having developed, together with Dale W. Jorgenson, the neoclassical theory of investment, in which a representative firm decides how much to invest based on the cost of capital. In this case, too, numerous empirical studies have contradicted his and Jorgenson’s neat theoretical findings: for firms’ investment choices depend primarily on expectations of future demand and the availability of financing sources such as bank credit. While Hall provided the theories for modeling the dynamics of aggregate consumption and investment, i.e., two fundamental components of GDP, Woodford played a prominent role in the “ New Neoclassical Synthesis ,” which sought to explain the dynamics of a capitalist economy. In his 2003 magnum opus Interest and Prices , Woodford developed a macroeconomic model called Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) based on the rational choices of a representative consumer and firm that maximize utility and profits, respectively, with perfect knowledge of the economic model in which they operate. The main difference between this DSGE model and those used by New Classical Macroeconomics is the existence of “market imperfections,” meaning monopolistic competition, and especially that firms do not change prices continuously. The presence of sticky prices thus allows the central bank to stabilize consumption, output, and employment by announcing its future policy decisions and changes in the interest rate. Thanks to this stickiness, monetary policy can influence GDP dynamics, even though the theoretical framework remains that of New Classical Macroeconomics. This compromise has often been referred to as “New Keynesianism,” and yet it has little to do with John Maynard Keynes’s work. Economic fluctuations, in fact, stem from shocks external to the model that temporarily push the economy away from market equilibrium, and only price rigidities allow monetary policy to correct these deviations. In contrast, for Keynes, economic cycles are an intrinsic feature of how capitalist systems function even in the presence of flexible prices. In this context, monetary policies, and especially fiscal policies, play a fundamental role in mitigating the lasting effects of financial crises and recessions. From the Great Moderation to the Great Recession The advent of the New Neoclassical Synthesis fueled growing confidence in macroeconomic models, seemingly confirmed by the so-called Great Moderation: a long period beginning in the mid-1980s, when many advanced economies saw a major reduction in the volatility of GDP and inflation. Many economists regarded this outcome as a “divine coincidence,” due in large part to improved monetary policy that slavishly followed the “scientific” principles provided by DSGE models. In this climate of optimism, reminiscent of Francis Fukuyama’s “End of History” thesis, Nobel laureate Robert Lucas solemnly declared, like some modern-day Pangloss, that economists had solved the problem of depressions. And in August 2008, Olivier Blanchard described the state of macroeconomics as “good.” Unfortunately, the outcome of this story is well known: in the fall of 2008, the subprime mortgage crisis plunged the global economy into the most severe recession since the Great Depression of 1929. Beneath the apparent stability indicated by DSGE models, inequality, household debt, and the fragility of banks and financial intermediaries were on the rise, while the financial sector was being deregulated, and new derivative products were being invented. Price stability masked the growing instability of the financial system. This all happened amid the utter silence of the dominant macroeconomic theory, which paid no attention to the behavior of banks and large investors. It did not acknowledge the possibility of a financial crisis, even as a theoretical prospect. As noted by Joseph Stiglitz and Paul Krugman , the failure to account for finance rendered the dominant models useless not only for predicting a crisis but also for explaining why it had emerged. Worse, DSGE models proved useless in formulating the economic policy interventions needed to avert a new depression, such as bank bailouts, expansionary fiscal policies, unconventional monetary policies, macroprudential regulations of the financial system, and extraordinary measures to prevent the collapse of financial markets. In essence, the contributions of Hall and Woodford and the New Neoclassical Synthesis more generally provided no theoretical foundation for macroeconomic stabilization. Instead they helped blind many economists and policymakers to the signs of the perfect storm that was about to hit the global economy. And when the crisis erupted, they proved inadequate for devising the economic policies needed to save global economies. An Extremely Fine-Grained, Imaginary World The main strength of DSGE models, which have become the dominant language of modern macroeconomics and influential tools within central banks, is their formal rigor. But mathematical consistency is no guarantee of realism. A model can rigorously describe what would happen in an imaginary world if the underlying assumptions were true, yet be totally unreliable when those assumptions are tested against reality. MIT economist Ricardo Caballero explained this clearly in the wake of the 2008 crisis. He showed how mainstream macroeconomics had become captivated by the models’ own internal logic, confusing the precision achieved in the virtual world they constructed with knowledge of the real world. This fed the risky assumption that existing policies would guarantee price and economic stability even as the conditions for the subprime mortgage crisis were being created. If the financial system is treated as marginal, and failures are either absent or greatly simplified, the model can provide extremely detailed answers to the wrong questions. As early as 2002, research at the Bank for International Settlements had shown that financial imbalances can grow even with low inflation, while economists Òscar Jordà, Alan Taylor, and Moritz Schularick found that rapid credit growth could signal systemic risks prior to a crisis. Still, this type of analysis remained on the margins of the dominant paradigm. To quote former Bank of England economist Charles Goodheart , the standard DSGE model excludes everything relevant to the stability of the financial system and “has been completely useless as a guide to the recent financial crisis.” Unfortunately, this trend has become more entrenched in mainstream macroeconomics ever since the theories developed in the 1970s by Robert Lucas and Thomas Sargent. The focus is, in fact, on mathematical elegance at the expense of critical analysis of the assumptions and the realism of the model. But the implications for economic policy depend on the assumptions, not on mathematical proofs derived from imaginary economies. Otherwise, we risk entrusting our understanding of macroeconomic dynamics and economic policy to “post-real” models, as Paul Romer wryly put it in 2016. After 2008, DSGE models incorporated imperfections in the credit market and homeopathic doses of heterogeneity among consumers. And Woodford himself addressed the relationship between monetary policy and financial stability. These are developments worth acknowledging. But adding a new host of frictions is not enough to explain how economic imbalances can lead to financial crises and deep recessions. The Cost of Orthodoxy and the Need for Pluralism There is also a less visible cost than the one directly involving economic crisis: namely, the stifling of pluralism in research. The theoretical-political construct developed around Hall’s and Woodford’s framework has become so dominant and self-referential that it has dismissed nearly all opposing arguments. Keynesian approaches as well as those of other economic schools, which focused on deep uncertainty, effective demand, income distribution, institutions, and financial instability, have often been deemed less scientific and marginalized. This not because they are contradicted by the data, but because they fall outside the language of the dominant paradigm, which lends a veneer of formal rigor. Krugman highlighted this paradox in 2016, asking what accurate predictions justified the hegemony of DSGE models. He noted how this methodology had sidelined less sophisticated analyses that were, however, more useful for understanding crises. This is not an objection to technical rigor but to the transformation of a particular technique into a dogmatic criterion for belonging to the discipline, where the dominant theory becomes almost a creed or, worse, a sect. And when the method matters more than the phenomena to be explained and the results obtained, the supposed rigor becomes a weapon to silence alternative theories. This occurs through control of scientific journals, where the guardians of orthodoxy publish only articles aligned with the relevant theoretical paradigm. In this way, as James Heckman and Sidharth Moktan argue , the careers of young economists are shaped, careerism is encouraged, and creativity is stifled. And all of this, according to George Akerlof , has discouraged research on financial crises, which were considered a secondary issue within the dominant paradigm — at least until the crisis struck. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics pays homage to a seductive idea. It suggests that, given an elegant theoretical model, the fluctuations of capitalist economies can be easily smoothed out through economic policies designed according to “scientific” principles. The problem is that reality cannot be bent to fit the model if the model represents a leap beyond economics, as asserted by Robert Solow. Different theoretical approaches are needed, therefore, like those that view economies as complex evolving systems. We can only hope that the awarding of the Nobel Prize to Hall and Woodford will spark a debate leading to greater pluralism in the field of economics, rewarding the ability to explain the real world rather than the formalism of imaginary worlds. Unfortunately, this too may be a little overoptimistic. articles.title: Groundwork and the Limits of Left Pragmatism
articles.content: R&R member Nikoli Weir writes on the political contradictions of Groundwork, rooted in the influence of bourgeois pragmatism. Signed articles do not necessarily represent the collective views of Reform & Revolution. The socialist left is in crisis. It has, for the past several decades, failed to provide a serious alternative to the current state of affairs. It has produced mountains of criticism of the present state of things, much of which is necessary and correct in its challenge to the dominant worldview, but which does not provide a program and strategy for our political moment. It is composed in large part by isolated, high-control sects that act more like guardians of the faith than a mass political formation. In response to the impotence of much of the organized left, there has emerged a bold, anti-tradition futurism which professes to go beyond the stale formulas of the representatives of revolutionary tradition. More often than not, it ends up falling into unprincipled opportunism. As the socialist movement expands and contracts, it tends to fluctuate between these two poles: uninspiring reliance on tradition on the one hand, and a “new, pragmatic” opportunism on the other. The result is that at any given time, the socialist left is held hostage by each of its two caricatures. “Pragmatism”, in this context, refers to a political framework that prioritizes working within currently existing political structures, not for the purpose of transforming or undermining them, but because doing so appears to be taking the path of least resistance, the path that “works” more than the others. There are endless examples of the former, missionary-style model from all over the Marxist political spectrum, ranging from the far-flung fragments of Trotskyism to the various Stalinist and Maoist organizations. In the United States, organizations like the People’s Defense Committee (PDC) seek to build dual power at the workplace and neighborhood level which can then serve as the basis for a new revolutionary social order. Their primary form of political activity, however, is the same charity work conducted by any number of churches or local Food Not Bombs groups. Examples of the latter, amorphous tendency are harder to pin down, in considerable part due to the content of their politics. They can take an ultra-left or reformist form depending on circumstance. This back-and-forth tendency exists most clearly within the Democratic Socialists of America. This is in part due to the structure of DSA itself, which encourages the formation of factions and caucuses based on common political interests among members. This is a good thing, as it allows these tendencies to be discussed in an environment of free and fair debate connected to mass organizing. Let’s examine a tendency that, in my view, perfectly demonstrates the pseudo-innovative opportunism characteristic of the “pragmatic” tendency in socialist politics. I will, in a later article, address sectarianism, but next time instead of analyzing a caucus, we will talk about a specific DSA chapter. Out of all of the currently active tendencies in DSA, the Groundwork Caucus most exemplifies the opportunist and vacillating tendency within the American Marxist left. Unlike many other DSA caucuses which either emerged out of a pre-existing political tradition (Bread and Roses, Reform and Revolution, Liberation, etc), Groundwork belongs to another category of those which seek to establish their own tendency and tradition, alongside Marxist Unity Group and Mountain Caucus. Groundwork is particularly eclectic in contrast to MUG’s interest in the Second International’s revolutionary period and Mountain’s Gramscianism. The “Groundwork Thought” library brings together Hal Draper, Ralph Milliband, Geese magazine, Fidel Castro, and more. This theoretical amorphism is carried directly into Groundwork’s practical work. Take, for example, Groundwork’s position on the leadership of the labor movement, which they spell out in their 2026 “Tasks and Perspectives” document. Groundwork embraces “working with union leadership when it advances the socialist project, and contesting for power within union leadership when it does not.” Groundwork claims that “union leadership…is deeply heterogeneous—with some leaders closely aligned with our goals, others fiercely opposed, and still others in between.” They go on to say that the socialist movement should “consider collaborating with leadership where we believe working together will help build longer-term class alignment and achieve our short-to-medium term goals, and consider organizing to replace that leadership in unions that actively obstruct the socialist project.” It goes without saying that our attitude towards and willingness to work with the leadership of unions should be determined by whether or not doing so will advance the cause of socialism. However, what needs to be answered before we can answer the question of working with union leadership is the following; what is the position of the leadership in the class struggle between workers and capitalists? Do union leaders and bureaucrats have more in common with the workers in their unions, or with the bosses who they are supposed to be fighting against? Furthermore, we must ask whether the things held in common are primarily ideological, organizational, or class interests. Though the existing union bureaucracy and its leaders are not themselves capitalists, their immediate interests often align more with the capitalists and their managerial servants than they do with the workers that they are supposed to represent. Union leaders, like managers and foremen, are separated from the production process. Both make significantly more money than the workers below them. And most importantly, both more often than not share an interest in preserving the status quo, as their social position depends on the stable flow of dues. The capitalists tolerate the little influence that the labor bureaucrats have in the workplace and wider society because the labor bureaucrats have historically stifled the workers’ movement by suppressing union democracy and opposing attempts to introduce class-struggle politics onto the shop floor. International Brotherhood of Teamsters president Sean O’Brien speaking at the 2024 Republican National Convention. (Photo: Will Lanzoni/CNN) Because the social position of the bureaucracy depends on the continued existence of the union, it is contradictory in character and can sometimes be compelled to act in defense of working-class interests. As a result, there exists a reformist or “left” wing of the bureaucracy, exemplified by United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain and many local labor leaders, who support democratic reforms such as open bargaining and are often friendly to socialists. While socialists can and should work with these figures on a united-front basis, relying on them can render socialists and union militants dependent on their whims. This dependence will inevitably undermine the struggle for democracy and socialism by placing the left on the side of the “progressive” apparatus against the rank-and-file. There are also those within the bureaucracy who use the language of militancy and class independence for cynical and reactionary purposes, such as Sean O’Brien of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Though Groundwork is correct in saying that the views of the labor leadership are heterogeneous, it fails to see that it is not about the orientation of this or that leader; it is about the class relations that the labor bureaucrats exist within, which create structures that incentivize them to act against the interests of the workers that they are supposed to represent. The fact that Teamsters for a Democratic Union, one of the most longstanding and influential union reform caucuses, still supports O’Brien after his open support for Trumpism is a powerful warning against illusions in left-talking bureaucrats. It seems that Groundwork’s hedged position exists solely to justify the caucus’s wavering on the question of the labor bureaucracy. This indecisiveness is present in their electoral strategy just as much as their views on union work. In the same “Tasks and Perspectives” document, Groundwork lays out two different approaches to electoral activity in DSA. On one end, you have the “left” approach, which seeks to use elections and elected offices as primarily bully pulpits to agitate and organize the working class. On the other end, elected office is fundamentally seen as a way to pass reforms that would improve the immediate quality of life for the working class. Under this model, according to Groundwork, candidates are “given leeway to operate independently coordinated DSA strategy, and sometimes even excused for taking stands that run counter to the will of the organization.” So, which of these two contradictory approaches is correct, according to Groundwork? Both! We contend that both of these approaches to electoral work get something right and something wrong, and that the best path forward entails a productive synthesis of these positions. Our strategy for building socialism entails winning and wielding state power to pass transformative reforms; as such, we reject the idea of running candidates to agitate and politicize rather than to win. At the same time, we believe candidates and socialists in office should work within a coordinated strategy set democratically by DSA members at the local, regional and national level, and that our races should popularize socialism and build the organization. Immediately we see that Groundwork’s electoral position is structured in the exact same way as their position on labor. At first glance, it appears very close to Reform & Revolution’s position on the role of struggles for immediate economic and democratic demands in rebuilding a mass socialist movement. However, once you look at Groundwork’s actual role within electoral work in DSA, it becomes clear that their position is reformist in character. Groundwork’s “middle-ground” position is reflective of the destructive influence of pragmatism in the socialist movement. For evidence of this, look no further than Groundwork’s position on whether or not NYC-DSA should have re-endorsed AOC for Congress in the midterm elections. AOC has for multiple years consistently betrayed the movement and organization that she claims to champion. She has run cover for the Biden Administration’s horrendous lies about “working towards a ceasefire in Gaza”; she has voted consistently to continue funding Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defense system, which provides literal cover for Israel to terrorize the Middle East with no fear of serious retaliation; in 2022, under the Biden Administration, she voted to break the then ongoing rail strike, which constituted one of the largest such strikes in decades. Not only that, but this vote went directly against DSA’s stated position, and she was admonished by name by the National Political Committee, who said as follows: “We disagree and are disappointed with the decision of DSA members Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and and Rep. Cori Bush to needlessly vote to enforce the [tentative agreement]… the members are the union and a majority of members voted to reject the [tentative agreement]. Socialist electeds must stand with unions when they reject a [tentative agreement].” With all of this in mind, it seems clear that, based on their principles, Groundwork should have been against re-endorsing AOC. However, their actual position is just the opposite. In an article titled “The Case for NYC-DSA Endorsing AOC in 2026” , Groundwork openly acknowledges all of AOC’s offenses against both DSA and her constituents. Despite that, they maintain that “AOC is our best chance to achieve an arms embargo against Israel.” They argue that in 2028, the likely Democratic frontrunners will be Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, and AOC. Out of those three options, they argue that AOC is the most likely person to implement an arms embargo against Israel, and that if we want to give her campaign as much steam as possible, that we should ensure she is re-elected to the House of Representatives in the mid term elections. This is despite the fact she has gone back on her word multiple times, and despite the fact that she isn’t a cadre candidate, both of which are acknowledged by Groundwork. In spite of this, they supported a congressional re-endorsement for AOC on the basis that not doing so would “damage [our] relationship, and would likely shut the door for a national DSA endorsement for 2028.” Unlike much of the DSA “left,” Reform & Revolution recognizes that we cannot simply will an independent left presidential campaign into existence. We recognize, with Groundwork, that AOC is (at this point in time) the only plausible left-labor candidate for the 2028 elections. This is where our agreement with Groundwork reaches its limits. For R&R, DSA’s involvement in AOC’s campaign should primarily be about DSA, not AOC. We should use the AOC campaign to organize people into DSA, advocate for and spread our views and our program, and build up a strong working-class political formation that can effectively outweigh the opportunism of AOC, which she will inevitably bring with her into the Oval Office. DSA’s intervention in a future AOC presidential run isn’t about “access” to power, it’s about how we can use the levers of mass political engagement to build power. At the end of the day, the fundamental difference is if such a campaign is run for AOC’s sake, or for DSA’s. Groundwork uses the language of pragmatism to claim that they are in fact in favor of running class-struggle campaigns, while also running campaigns on a limited, reformist basis. But where are these “class-struggle campaigns” that Groundwork believes are so important to the movement? Why is it that, when push comes to shove, Groundwork always prioritizes the reformist and opportunist approach over the class-struggle approach? Why is it that DSA’s “coordinated strategy,” to use Groundwork’s own words, is also sacrificed for the sake of reformism and opportunism? It is quite simple. The class-struggle approach to electoralism is sacrificed for the reformist approach, because that is the point of the vagueness of Groundwork’s position. This “pragmatic” approach allows Groundwork to claim to support bold, independent tactics in instances where doing so “works,” while never actually doing so, under the guise of there being no plausible class-struggle campaigns to wage. Because the class-struggle path is seemingly “unworkable,” it allows Groundwork to always put it off into the future. Not this campaign, but the next one! We aren’t ready now, but soon we will be! And the moment we are ready, we will do what needs to be done. That moment naturally never comes, so Groundwork continues doing what they always do. This is opportunism par excellence , and it can be seen in every one of Groundwork’s major positions. Not only that, but this can be seen whenever opportunism is the dominant approach to politics, whether it be in the German Social Democrats in the 20s, the Communist Party USA in the 30s, or today’s reformists in DSA. Groundwork’s opportunism can be explained within the framework of the Triple Crisis and Dual Task. Traditionally, Trotskyists have maintained that the crisis of our age is a crisis of leadership; that is, the working class movement is failing to meet the moment because its leadership in the political parties and the trade unions is opportunist, reformist, or deficient in some other way. Because of this emphasis, Trotskyists have historically focused on building up revolutionary cores within mass movements, revolutionary cores who work patiently to win the mantle of leadership away from the bourgeois reformists and labor bureaucrats and lead the workers to victory in the battle for democracy. Though R&R continues to recognize the crisis of leadership as playing a central role in our organizing work, we expand it to include two other crises; the crisis of organization and the crisis of consciousness. The truth of the matter is that the conditions of the 21st century are radically different from the conditions in which Trotsky first laid out the crisis of leadership. The 1930s were a period where the working-class movement was much more developed politically and organizationally, a time of mass parties and mass struggles; it was, theoretically, possible for a small core of revolutionaries to make qualitative leaps toward mass influence in a short period of time. Right now, the situation is very different. The working-class parties and organizations formed in the early and mid 20th century have been neutered and destroyed by decades of austerity and counter-insurgency. The working class as a political subject has spent years in disarray, often not even recognizing itself as a class with class-specific interests and goals. Union membership in the United States has been at an all time low for a long time, and the sphere of mass organization necessary to scaffold a political project, to foster a class worldview and class social bonds, is extremely weak. In the past few years genuine progress has been made. Promising new unions have cropped up in industries that have historically been unorganized, like Starbucks Workers United and the Amazon Labor Union. DSA, which is by a large margin the only relevant socialist organization in the US doing national work, can boast some major wins, such as electing its candidate to the New York City Mayor’s office and breaching 130,000 members. However, despite these successes, the crises of leadership, organization and consciousness remain. If any progress is to be made in surmounting these strategic problems, then we must address them simultaneously. The crises are dialectically interrelated with each other, and any attempt to address one without addressing the others will kneecap the movement. It is this that is the source of Groundwork’s errors. Groundwork focuses exclusively on resolving the crisis of organization, choosing to rely on an amorphous political pragmatism, a “whatever works, works” approach to party-building. This pragmatism does not interrogate what it means for something to “work,” or who and what it is working for. It assumes that anything that builds DSA numerically is good. This results in them having a strong base of active members who are able and willing to participate in the struggles of the day, but who often have difficulty correctly analyzing the problems that caused the crisis and chartering plausible paths forward. This in part explains Groundwork’s theoretical confusion, which we have already discussed. Of course a caucus that prioritizes the development of DSA’s immediate organizational capacity above all other considerations will end up adopting confused, contradictory positions. The confusion and contradiction are not errors; they are on purpose. A position that is in reality a non-position, that can go whichever way the wind blows, serves Groundwork perfectly. It allows them to hold radical principles in theory, while in reality giving them leeway to subordinate their principles for the sake of growing DSA. Here we get to the key point: you cannot meaningfully and effectively grow an organization like DSA by sacrificing its long-term aims and principles for short-term publicity and influence. This will backfire, every time. DSA as an organization does not exist to serve itself. It exists to advance the cause, aims and principles of socialism. Without those principles and ideas, and without an independent working-class political base, DSA means nothing. We could, right now, sacrifice all of our principles, totally cave to the establishment Democrats, and go all in on becoming an organ of the Democratic Party. If we did this, it is likely that we could get quite a few paper members elected to local and state legislatures all across the country, and maybe even build a large socialist bloc in Congress. But would it be worth it? Would it really be a win for DSA if in order to achieve this we had to sacrifice everything that makes DSA what it is? One suspects that Groundwork knows the answer is “no.” It is very possible that Groundwork’s approach “works,” if by “works” we mean succeeds in gaining recognition and members for DSA. But what then? For what purpose does Groundwork wish to build DSA? For what purpose does Groundwork seek to elect socialists to office? These are not ends in themselves. They are means to the end of the socialist transformation of society. If we elect members to all levels of government, but they do nothing more than trail the “progressive” Democrats, we may as well have not elected them at all. If we recruit thousands of members, only to funnel them into doorknocking campaigns for “socialists” who are reluctant to even declare themselves as such, and who are nearly indistinguishable from progressive liberals like Brad Lander, we might as well have not recruited them at all. Our end goal isn’t to endlessly elect socialists into office. Our goal is to transform American society by means of a mass socialist movement. To that end, we run DSA candidates in elections, with the understanding that bourgeois elections are a means to spread our message, advance transitional demands and structural reforms, and use elected office as a bully pulpit to organize the masses. The moment we confuse the means with the ends is the moment that we cease to be a fighting organization of the working class whose aim is the total transformation of society, and become a social-humanitarian group whose highest aspiration is the passing of ultimately inadequate reforms that do nothing to address the root cause of our social ills.

articles.title: Thomas Frank on How the Promise of Progress Soured
articles.author: Thomas Frank
articles.content: The pundit and cultural historian Thomas Frank has again done what he does best: holding up an unflattering mirror to the extreme center. Where the object lesson of Frank’s 2016 book, Listen, Liberal , was the Democratic Party’s neoliberal, technocratic turn, and in his 2020 work, The People, No , he examined how populism turned from a lived political ideology into a self-serving cuss word, in his new book, The Creativity Con , Frank has unpicked the chattering classes’ infatuation with all things innovative. As the title gives away, that obsession has produced a con. The book traces the history of creativity thinking in the United States. Frank picks up the thread in the early twentieth century when some ad men (BBDO cofounder Alex Osborn is key here) promised US workers that creativity was a democratic virtue and that everyone could hone their abilities to come up with something new. Frank traces the story all the way to the likes of Richard Florida, who, as an academic and consultant, became rich and influential by selling town halls the world over policy recipes to remake their desolate, deserted neighborhoods into shiny launchpads for the creative class. Ideas, knowledge, and brainpower were supposed to become the commodities of the twenty-first century, while jobs “bending metal” had become the obsolete purview of the losers, the poor, and the uneducated. What was needed to attract the creatives, Florida explained, were lofts and bike paths and lattes, while the plight of the metal benders was treated as an afterthought. Frank takes us all the way to the present, with its return of geopolitical conflict and its shadow of technological disruption hanging over the life prospects even of the academically certified. He invites us readers to follow him along with his hilarious reportage (at South by Southwest), deep digs in libraries and archives (Alex Osborn again), and trips to cities where Florida and his ilk sold their magic. We also join Frank in parsing US presidential speeches filled to the brim with “innovation blather” (which he calls “innotalk”) and see him deconstruct weapons’ producers marketing material — in the process taking a swipe at Marianna Mazzucato’s modern classic The Entrepreneurial State for failing to note that all those big beautiful public innovations from Silicon Valley were meant to maim, kill, and destroy. These observations are interspersed with Frank’s more personal ruminations: on the world’s fairs his parents took him to; onthe fate of his artist friends in a world where Spotify has turned the music industry into a winner-takes-all market; and on the goals and aims of The Baffler , the countercultural magazine that he and friends set up in 1988. In its second part, the book pivots from a critical cultural history to a pamphlet of critical political economy. There Frank contrasts the shiny marketing rhetoric of the creatives and innovators with the material reality they have created. His verdict: the narrative of the United States as the harbinger of newness is, worse than bullshit, a camouflage to obscure that the best times lie not ahead of us but in the past. He concludes that what he calls “progressland” has actually produced a country in decline. For Jacobin , Ewald Engelen spoke with Frank about the function of “innotalk,” artificial intelligence, the midterms, the blue wave, cynicism, and the need to save the past from the future. Ewald Engelen The key to the book is the flip halfway through from scathing social criticism to the real world “innotalk” has produced. You describe its function as providing camouflage. Explain? Thomas Frank The word is used by different people to mean different things, but it’s always self-interested. It’s always performing some interest — it’s always some way of describing their interests as universal interests. But it does it by different methods. So, when Barack Obama uses the word “innovation,” it means something different than when defense contractors use it. But in both cases, they’re using it for really ugly purposes. Obama is using it to tell his base, Democratic voters, that he’s on board. He’s a progressive because it’s all about progress: innovation is progress. It’s change. And he’s also using it at the same time to tell Google: I hear you. I get it. So, it’s a word that’s extremely useful for him because he gets to have it both ways. But then with the defense contractors, it’s camouflage for their project, which is to loot the taxpayer. And the Pentagon — who really cares about national defense? These billion-dollar airplanes and destroyers that cost as much as nuclear aircraft carriers, these crazy things that always come with massive cost overruns and fail to perform: that’s not what this is about. It’s about pocketing the spoils of war. No more, no less. Ewald Engelen Your exercise in unmasking depends crucially on the 2016 book by the US economic historian Robert Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth . In it, he argues that productivity growth has stagnated since the late 1970s and that Big Tech, the smartphone, and the internet have failed to show up in productivity statistics. Is that still the case? What about the AI bubble and the potential wipeout of the creative class? Thomas Frank Wouldn’t that be something? After all these years, finally, finally. That would be appropriate, because I just finished working on this big project saying it hasn’t happened, and it would be hilarious if then it finally did happen right after I put the book out. So, I don’t know. Maybe tomorrow it’ll finally arrive. But look: productivity growth is nowhere near where it was in the 1940s or 1950s or 1960s. Maybe next year it will be, but we haven’t seen it so far. However, I have my doubts, for obvious reasons. There’s still a lot of brilliance in the world. There are still a lot of people coming up with new things. It’s just that the incentives are all arranged in such a way that the things they come up with do not add to the general wealth of the country. They add to the personal wealth of a small handful of people. We’ve arranged the incentives in a way that the general public and the economy as a whole don’t benefit much from all the stuff that people have dreamed up. Ewald Engelen The Creativity Con appeared a couple of weeks before the midterms. Did you see any signs on the side of Democrats that they have dropped “innotalk” and have shifted to a language of material needs? Thomas Frank Not in those terms, no. Nobody has. But indirectly, yes. There’s massive backlash against AI and the data centers. And also, Donald Trump’s basically aligning himself with the billionaire elite, specifically Elon Musk. Right now, Jensen Huang was in the news because he was basically [Trump’s] second-best friend after Elon. All of that really came back to bite him, thank goodness. The other thing that’s interesting is Barack Obama, who is still regarded and probably will be forever regarded by most Democrats as something of a saint. So, I went to the opening day at the Obama library. In it, he has reimagined his own history so that he is the descendant and legatee of all the great reform movements of the past. He is the culmination of the civil rights movement. He’s the culmination of the women’s suffrage movement. He’s the culmination of progressivism. He’s the culmination of the antiwar movement of the 1960s. All these things. There’s this elaborate museum, and the first story of the museum is all about these various left-wing social movements of the past. And they all lead to this one guy, Barack Obama. The exhibit on innovation is on the top story. He doesn’t leave it out, but it’s not emphasized as much as it was during his presidency — implying that his faith in innovation has now gone out of fashion. Ewald Engelen What about the Financial Times claiming that the Democrats won because they replaced identity-talk with class-talk? Thomas Frank Well, yes. In that sense, it’s a good thing. In that sense, yes, I’m very hopeful about it. But these are the Democrats we’re talking about. They will disappoint you every time. Look, I’m sixty-one years old. I’ve been a very cynical person. And cynicism has served me pretty well. So, I’m not going to all of a sudden say, “We’ve turned a corner and this is great.” By the way, the centrist faction in the Democratic Party is fighting back pretty hard right now. And they’re claiming that the election was not about those things. It was actually about their things. This is what they do in America. They have an election, and then they fight about what it actually meant. Ewald Engelen In the book, you call yourself a scoffer by trade. Why? Thomas Frank That’s pure H. L. Mencken, the Baltimore newspaper man. He had this very witty, scathing, vicious style. A man of incredible perceptiveness, but who had really lousy politics, really kind of ugly libertarian politics. He hated everything and everybody, he but had this astonishing power to penetrate the surface of things. I read him starting in high school and was always convinced that that was missing from the way the Left talked, the way the Left wrote about politics back in the day when I started. It’s also an automatic stance of skepticism toward whatever you see on serious television or read in serious newspapers and whatever you hear on serious radio. There is no intellectual fun in debunking Fox News. There is in reading a New York Times op-ed from a mainstream political scientist professor against the grain. Ewald Engelen The final sentence of the book reads: “Spotify pulls up the Clash for me, a creative work I remember not just liking, but believing in when I was 19. Yet somehow it sounds all wrong now, impossible to understand, some frantic noise from another age, another civilization, a world that is no more.” That is pure nostalgia, isn’t it? Thomas Frank What I am commenting upon here is directly taken from the British historian E. P. Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class , where at the end he talks about saving the past from the “enormous condescension of posterity.” His book, as well as mine, is a clarion call against forgetfulness, against obsolescence — the obsolescence of humans as well as machines. And I was really feeling it. I was on vacation with my daughter. We were in Japan, and I was in an enormous train station in Tokyo. Enormous. And then Spotify, the machine, pulled up a song I was listening to when I was nineteen, bringing forcefully home the downside of progress: obsolescence, and also alienation and condescension. Our condescension for the past, in this culture — in the culture of progress, the culture where innovation is valued — our condescension for the past is enormous. In some sense, I’ve always been that guy. I want to be like E.P. Thompson. I want to rescue these people from the condescension of posterity. And the nous and acumen and political courage of the historical populists are the classic case. articles.title: Reggio Emilia Stares Down an Uncertain Future
articles.author: Giulia Lasagni
articles.content: From early morning on August 3, around a hundred people placed themselves between machinery and 45,000 square meters of abandoned land on the eastern outskirts of Reggio Emilia, a northern Italian city about forty miles from Bologna. They came to prevent more than two hundred mature trees, dense undergrowth, and a pond from being cleared for a Conad supermarket. The project also included other planned buildings as well as parking, pavements, and bike lanes. The occupation, reached by a small road off the Via Emilia, quickly became a permanent encampment, with a field kitchen, tents, and nightly assemblies. About two months later, the area was cleared by police. The green space, now owned by the supermarket chain, was destroyed. The word bosco , woodland, was itself part of the battle. For developers, the site was abandoned land awaiting regeneration. For its defenders, the two decades of neglect had produced an urban forest that serves as badly needed green space in a city facing increasingly extreme weather. Bosco Ospizio poses the simple question of who really owns a site abandoned by both public authorities and private capital. Does it belong to the company that holds the deeds, to the city hall that approved its redevelopment, or to the people living with the consequences? The answer is controversial even locally. Many opposed the project and joined the campaign, while other residents supported redevelopment as a source of services, jobs, safety, and investment in an area they see as neglected. In Reggio Emilia, the question also carries unusual historical weight. The city was one of the great laboratories of Italy’s postwar Communist municipal left. For decades, the Emilia-Romagna region was celebrated for showing that Communists could govern democratically and effectively. Now it’s less clear that today’s left still has the same ability to resolve problems. The City as a Collective Project The “Emilian model” rested on strong municipalities, mass parties, trade unions, cooperatives, neighborhood organizations, and a dense associational culture. Political participation extended beyond elections through party branches, citizens’ committees, cultural associations, and negotiation between institutions and organized society. Urban planning was central. As postwar modernization transformed Emilia from an agricultural region into one of Europe’s most dynamic industrial economies, the Left faced the challenge of governing development, preventing speculation, and turning some of the newly generated wealth into public services. Planning meant deciding where people would live, how they would move, and which services they could access, regardless of income. The model shouldn’t be romanticized. It depended on party structures that were often hierarchical as well as participatory, and it treated economic growth as the central measure of success. Still, it also had a clear direction: public authority sought to shape the market and redistribute its gains. The city was understood as a collective political project. Bosco Ospizio points to an inversion of this relationship. The project was approved under a center-left mayor and carried forward by successive center-left administrations. In the Italian context, center-left refers to the convergence of different political traditions: not only the long-hegemonic Communist Party, but also the Catholic tradition of social reformism associated with Christian Democracy, particularly influential in Reggio Emilia through the legacy of Giuseppe Dossetti. In February 2026, city hall announced that building permits had been issued for the site. The proposal combines a 2,500-square-meter supermarket with a library, community hub, and health facilities, while retaining 23,000 square meters as public green space. This combination is the project’s strongest defense. Supporters see a practical compromise that would provide services, employment, and a safer, more accessible public space. Opponents argue that mature woodland, a pond, and established vegetation cannot be replaced by landscaping created after construction. “Public services are being delegated to a private entity,” one activist said. The problem is that the success of a commercial project here becomes the condition for obtaining collective infrastructure. The city hall may negotiate the details, grant permission, and promise mitigation measures, but it no longer commands the process; it only brokers it. Here as around Italy, local authorities have been squeezed for decades by fiscal restraint, privatization, and the erosion of their capacity to plan and invest directly. In this scenario, decisions about a neighborhood’s future migrate from the world of political programs and collective planning into business contracts, changes to urban planning, and negotiations with landowners. By the time residents ever get consulted, the fundamental choices may already have been made by others. “There had to be political will [for the Conad plan to go head],” this same activist said. Yet support for Bosco Ospizio shows that consultation cannot be dismissed as a mere exercise in managing dissent. The residents who support the project — prioritizing services, employment, safety, and the reuse of neglected land — surely do have a legitimate understanding of the public interest. For them, a library, health center, and supermarket may seem more valuable than preserving a site that was inaccessible or poorly maintained for years. The dispute is not simply, then, about whether Conad’s plan contains green space: it surely does. More than that, it raises the question of what kind of green space is needed, who defines its value, and whether the promised benefits justify destroying an existing ecosystem during a climate crisis. There is a further irony in this. For the supermarket Conad is not an alien multinational descending on a red city. Founded in Bologna in 1962 as a cooperative of independent retailers, the chain is still today organized through territorial cooperatives. While operating much like any other major supermarket chain, its cooperative origins point to a different economic and political tradition, one whose relationship with the territory has profoundly changed over time. It belongs, at least genealogically, to the same regional cooperative space that gave the Emilian model much of its rootedness in society. In this sense, too, the Bosco Ospizio is more widely revealing of the transformation of Emilia’s postwar institutions. The cooperative has itself become a major developer. The Communist municipality has become a center-left power broker. Citizens who once organized through mass politics now do so outside of such spaces, placing their bodies in front of construction machinery to reopen decisions that had formally been settled years earlier. Others accept or welcome the project as a practical response to local needs. In short, while the old institutions remain visible, the relationships involved in them have changed. A Mirror of the Left Today Bosco Ospizio is a small but unusually clear mirror of the Left’s wider predicament. For while center-left parties speak the language of equality, participation, and the ecological transition, their practice in government more often amounts to administering business as usual. This practice could easily be accused of hypocrisy. But more realistically, it is a reflection of a political model that prioritizes institutional competence over mass participation. As parties have retreated from workplaces and neighborhoods, their relationship with citizens has become thinner and more limited to election time. Political participation is only a fraction of what it once was. Public authorities, meanwhile, have lost resources, expertise, and confidence, becoming increasingly dependent on private actors to deliver investment. The Left may occupy the town hall, but it often lacks, or no longer tries to build, the social power needed to confront the interests shaping the city beyond it. If democratic participation cannot reopen a settled decision when ecological conditions, public priorities, and organized opinion have changed, then it becomes a kind of consultation without real consequences. And yet, if it ignores the residents who support the project, it also becomes exclusionary in a different way. The activists’ proposal to keep the green space revives a key feature of the Emilian tradition: planning as a democratic process while now updating that inheritance for a city that has been altered by the effects of climate change. The postwar left promised development with social protection. According to the Bosco activists, the Left today must recognize that existing nature is itself a form of essential infrastructure. We have said that the Emilian model ought not be romanticized. Its strength was not that the Communist mayors of old were exceptionally capable managers but lay in the fact that their administrations formed part of a larger attempt to shift power away from private wealth and toward organized citizens. This too is why Bosco Ospizio matters beyond Reggio Emilia. The idea of progressive municipalism is again in fashion today, from European cities confronting austerity to debates over what local government can and should do. The Emilian experience deserves attention in this regard, but not as a ready-made brand or as a success story worthy of nostalgia. At Bosco Ospizio, activists have forced these contradictions into the open. The battle over a patch of woodland has become a larger argument about what a city is for, whose needs count, and, ultimately, who gets to decide. articles.author: Austin Warrington
articles.content: In the wake of the midterms, the entirety of left-liberal America was jubilant. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, outperforming even the most idealistic predictions. But it was not only the Democratic victories that shocked observers — it was the kind of candidates who won. Democratic socialists had their strongest showing of any election in recent history, winning 169 endorsed ballot measures and seats at the local, state, and federal levels — their strongest showing of any general election in recent history. And the wins by nonsocialist progressives and even many centrists affirmed an agenda championed by democratic socialists, centering economic populism, wealth redistribution, and universal health care. But then a harsh reality set in: the near inevitability of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the House, a result that seemed to fly in the face of the progressive results we’d just seen. On Wednesday, just eleven Democrats voted against Jeffries in an internal nonbinding vote, including a bloc of five newly elected democratic socialists, joined by two additional Democrats. In a statement on their decision, the no voters cited ongoing negotiations around “Medicare for All, stopping [Immigration and Customs Enforcment (ICE)] terror, getting money out of politics, [and] ending the genocide in Gaza.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez notably did not join the no votes. Jeffries is decidedly not a leftist nor a progressive. He is a pro-corporate Democrat who defends Israel and readily takes American Israel Public Affairs Committee money and corporate money. How, in the face of such a resounding progressive message from voters, could there be no clear alternative? It’s understandable that some on the Left might feel deflated by this outcome. But we can also see the speaker conundrum as exposing an organizing void in Congress, one that the broadly left-leaning forces that felt so heartened by the midterm results have to confront soberly: we simply do not currently have the power, leverage, or internal relationships to elect a speaker that reflects the mandate we just witnessed. Changing that reality will need to start with an honest evaluation of the conditions surrounding the speakership race. Jeffries has spent years building up to this moment. The relationships he’s nurtured with his careful, deliberate style and results he’s delivered to the Democratic caucus — negotiating important earmarks for Democrats in a Republican-controlled House, leading a multistate campaign to neutralize Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts, and steering increasingly large fundraising hauls to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — were all leading to this moment. Any challenger, particularly one from a rising Left that is at its very beginnings in the halls of power, would be at a massive disadvantage. Not only that, but any defectors willing to stick their necks out to back an alternative would be putting a target on their back, as Jeffries plays a key role in committee assignments and setting the agenda for the floor. Asking our electeds to risk their ability to successfully carry out their jobs and advance our priorities would be irresponsible without a viable path to success. Socialists grappling with increasing power in government have to think long-term about how to create the conditions where a majority of House Democrats can back a socialist speaker. The time to start building toward that outcome is now, in Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) working groups and organizing committees across the country. Our bench of socialist electeds needs to be deeper in a way that can build buy-in for our goals among the general public, and we need to continue the work of relationship-building with our existing socialist electeds. Deepening our bench of electeds happens at every level of government and requires a clear-eyed assessment of what it takes to win races, which usually centers on an ambitious fundraising plan. Designated candidate recruitment organizers can begin by identifying prospective candidates and taking meetings now in anticipation of 2028; ideal candidates have preexisting ties to DSA or a labor union, direct organizing experience, a demonstrated commitment to advancing socialist policies, and a willingness to work collaboratively and meet regularly with chapter leaders once elected. Creating buy-in and demonstrating the popularity of our agenda among the public requires frequent and honest communication with the public. Rep. Ocasio-Cortez excels at this, making the often opaque operations of Congress accessible to millions through social media. To elect a socialist speaker, we would need to launch a campaign early, educating the public on the mechanisms as well as the stakes of the speaker’s race and building consensus around a candidate. A successful campaign will put us in a strong position when it is time for members to vote, where we can flex our organizing muscle to exert pressure using all of the support we’ve built throughout the course of the campaign. Most importantly, we will need to continue the work of building relationships with our bloc of socialist electeds across the country. This work is carried out by trusted organizing leaders in regularly scheduled group meetings . It necessitates strong interpersonal skills on both ends, including the ability to manage conflict healthily and negotiate. Chapters with maturing socialist coalitions should connect with the architects of more established programs to take some of the many lessons that have emerged over the years. What distinguishes democratic socialists from other politicians is that strategizing and organizing don’t stop after election day. The project of building power is year-round and relies on the active participation of skilled organizers working with elected officials. In the past two weeks, Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier have organized canvasses of their constituents, asking them directly what they should prioritize in Congress and who they should back as speaker. This ongoing dialogue with constituents represents a new kind of strategy — one in which elected officials meet people where they’re at to continue the work of organizing outside of an electoral context, facilitating dialogue at the doors and creating trust and buy-in. This is only a small piece of what it will take to win our agenda, but it is an important and meaningful step toward the kind of politics we should always be practicing: one that centers the needs of working people and ensures their voices echo in the halls of power. articles.title: Xi, Putin, and Trump meeting concludes with vague commitments, but strong symbolism
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first ever trilateral summit of Russia, China, and the US on the sidelines of the ongoing Asia-Pacific Economic Council (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19. The meeting, attended by Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, ended with a joint Declaration towards Peace with all three countries agreeing to find ways to work together on common issues including the need for reforms in the UN, global energy security, and rising nuclear risk. The declaration also talked about the principles of the operation of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and underlined the immunity for top state officials. The declaration emphasized that the reforms in the UN are necessary for it to make effective interventions to issues of global concern and to fulfill its mandate of preserving global peace and security. The point was an indirect reflection on recent failures of the UN to make any meaningful intervention in the global conflicts particularly its failure to prevent the Israel’s genocide in Gaza, the war in Ukraine and the US-Israeli war on Iran. All three countries also agreed that they should work together to reduce the risks of a nuclear war breaking out. They underlined the need to conduct dialogue for reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The three heads of states also agreed it was necessary to maintain the global flow of energy and to minimize the disruptions to global energy supply chains even during conflict and to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum to ease constraints on general production and prices. Thycydides trap is not destiny During his speech in the summit, hinting towards recent conflicts, Xi pointed out that there must be peace among major countries in the world in order to maintain global stability and to avoid chaos. Asking for a more friendly and trust based relations between the great power Xi denounced the conventional notions of great power rivalry repeating that the so-called “Thucydides Trap is by no means a destiny.” Thycydides, an ancient Greek historian, is often quoted to describe conflicts and rivalries between a rising power and an established one. As major countries and the permanent members of the UN Security Council China, Russia and the US must work together to meet global challenges and jointly uphold world peace and stability. They together can make greater contributions to the progress of humanity, Xi argued. Xi recalled how China, Russia and the US have worked together in the past to save the world from fascism during the Second World War claiming the same coordination is required now to “steadfastly safeguard the postwar international order, uphold the purposes and principles of the UN charter, and defend the hard-won outcomes.” Xi proposed a four point code of conduct for the great powers to work together; mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation and dialogue and consultation. For working together it is necessary that all the countries respect each other’s social structure and distinctive development paths adopted without trying to impose each other’s preferences over the other, Xi underlined. He also emphasized the UN principles of respecting each others’ sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference in domestic affairs as fundamental for good relations. “On major sensitive issues concerning one another, it is important to communicate in advance, try to see things from one another’s perspective, act with caution, and in particular, not to challenge the red lines of one another,” Xinhua reported Xi saying. Pointing towards the rising risks of nuclear conflicts and its possible impact on the existence of humanity, Xi talked about the need to push for complete nuclear disarmament. “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Domcleas that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons,” the Chinese leader said. Greater communication and coordination Indirectly referring to the impacts of US policies on global trade, Xi said that “decoupling and disruption of industrial and supply chains are not the ways to go” calling for stronger communication and coordination to “safeguard the security and stability of the global” markets. Both the US-Israeli war on Iran and Ukraine war have disrupted global supply chains of energy products. While Iran has restricted movements through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the US-Israeli war, Russia has been prevented from exporting freely due to sanctions and attacks on energy installations. Trump and Putin agreed with Xi’s call for a joint effort to push the countries to resolve their disputes through diplomatic channels with Putin emphasizing on “shared responsibilities” and calling for “proper resolution” of all “hotspot issues.” Trump claimed the three countries, the biggest military powers with the largest number of nuclear arsenals in the world, were “making history” by correcting a historical mistake of great powers not talking to each other.
