articles.title: “Historic Judgment”: World Court Rules Burma Guilty of Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Later in the broadcast, we’ll speak with three leading environmental justice advocates, from Malaysia, from Ethiopia and from India. But right now we go to this top story out of The Hague. This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. In a historic decision, the International Court of Justice in The Hague has ruled Myanmar, also known as Burma, committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. It’s the first time the court has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The presiding judge of the International Court, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, read the ruling. JUDGE YUJI IWASAWA : For these reasons, the court, one, by nine votes to six, finds that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. … The court has also determined that the estimate of 10,000 Rohingya violently killed during those clearance operations is supported by the evidence. … On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state. AMY GOODMAN : The genocide case against Burma, or Myanmar, was brought by The Gambia, the smallest country in mainland Africa. Gambia’s Justice Minister Dawda Jallow spoke in The Hague after the ruling. DAWDA JALLOW : Today, the International Court of Justice confirmed what Rohingya have said since 2017: What was done to them was genocide, and Myanmar is responsible. The court has found that Myanmar breached the 1948 convention, Genocide Convention, and has ordered to make reparations. This is the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide, the crime of crimes. The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed. AMY GOODMAN : The International Court of Justice, ICJ , case was closely followed in Bangladesh, where more than 1.2 million Rohingya Muslim refugees live after being forcibly displaced from their homes. Rahama Khatun is a 43-year-old Rohingya widow living in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. RAHAMA KHATUN : [translated] My husband was killed in the Rakhine area. I want justice for his murder. Following this verdict, I am now demanding exemplary punishment for those who killed my husband. I hope the perpetrators will receive the punishment they deserve. … We hope to return to Myanmar one day. However, for a safe and dignified return, our homes and lands must be restored, adequate compensation must be provided, and our fundamental rights and citizenship must be guaranteed. Our children must also be given access to education. AMY GOODMAN : While Bangladesh is home to the most Rohingya refugees, there are also sizable populations in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, United Arab Emirates, India and here in Turkey. Earlier today, Malaysia announced it’ll resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees in Turkey. Thursday’s historic ruling comes as the International Court of Justice is also in the process of determining whether Israel committed genocide in Gaza, in a case brought by South Africa. We’re joined now by two guests. Philippe Sands served on The Gambia’s legal team. His piece in The New York Times today is headlined “Can a Country Be Guilty of Genocide? Finally, the Answer Is Yes.” Philippe Sands is a professor of law at University College London and a visiting professor at Harvard Law School. He’s also the author of East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity . We are also joined in London by Maung Zarni. He’s a Burmese dissident and co-author of the 2014 study headlined “The Slow-Burning Genocide of Myanmar’s Rohingya.” He’s a human rights activist and scholar of genocide. Maung Zarni, let’s begin with you. Can you respond to the ICJ decision, the first time the court has held a country responsible for genocide? MAUNG ZARNI : Yes. This is a vindication of what Rohingyas have been saying for the last almost 50 years, since 1978, when the first wave of genocidal expulsion was conducted by the very same perpetrating institution, Myanmar military. The Rohingyas were the first to actually frame their experience, those who survived the first wave, under the false pretext of illegal immigration crackdown in February 1978, as genocide. But they have not been believed. And many of us who started looking at this from a both historical and sociological, not just legal, perspective of genocide, which is a coordinated process of group destruction based on identity, have been saying it. And so, yesterday, the court ruling simply vindicated what Rohingyas have known for decades to be a genocidal persecution of their group simply because of their identity. They are killed, their community is uprooted and destroyed, simply because they are Rohingya. Genocide is an identity-based group destruction. And so the court vindicated Rohingya’s collective articulation, memory and sufferings. AMY GOODMAN : If you could, Zarni, describe the condition on the ground, both in Bangladesh, that has more than a million Rohingya who have fled their country, Burma, and the conditions on the ground in a country that the ICJ , the International Court of Justice, has determined has committed a genocide against the Rohingya. MAUNG ZARNI : Well, in Bangladesh, the, like you said, Amy, 1.2 million Rohingya genocide survivors — they are not simply displaced people from Myanmar, as the Bangladeshi government described it — that they live in, you know, semi-Gaza-like situation, except without the daily bombings and cutting off deliberately of food rations and access to humanitarian aid. I’ve been there a number of times, and, like, just a month after they were driven out, about 700 — over 700,000 were driven out in the months of August, September and October in 2017. And, you know, they have no future. You know, the resettlement is not an option. They are trapped in these refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar. Inside Myanmar, about half a million Rohingyas are living under military occupation, not of — not the Myanmar military, but another anti-Muslim, anti-Rohingya Buddhist racist group called Arakan Army, representing Buddhist Rakhine in the region of Rakhine state, which is shared by both Rohingya, predominantly Muslims, and Rakhine ethnic group, largely Buddhist. And, you know, they’re under military occupation. And then you’ve got another population of diaspora in Malaysia, about 100,000. They are subject to all kinds of hate mobilization by the Malaysian groups. And so, you know, when we talk about Rohingya, we need to look at, like, three different populations that have survived and suffer all kinds of hardships and, you know, repression: in diaspora, refugee camps and still inside Myanmar. AMY GOODMAN : I want to turn to Philippe Sands, who is on The Gambia’s legal defense team at the International Court of Justice. First of all, Philippe, why The Gambia? Why did they bring this case? And number two, talk about the significance, again, of this being the first country that has been convicted of genocide, and what that ultimately means. PHILIPPE SANDS : Sure. Well, it’s lovely to be back on with you after a gap of about 15 years, Amy. The Rohingya case was brought by The Gambia basically on the initial instance of a single individual, Ba Tambadou, who was the attorney general of The Gambia, who went on a visit to Cox’s Bazar, the place that’s just been described, spoke to a lot of the people who had fled Myanmar, heard stories, and because he had been previously a prosecutor in the Rwanda Criminal Tribunal in The Hague, in Arusha, understood that the stories that he was being told told a story of genocide. He persuaded the government of The Gambia, of which he was a member, to bring a case to the International Court of Justice. One of the reasons that happened is because both Myanmar and Gambia were parties to the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of Genocide, and The Gambia is predominantly a Muslim country concerned about the mistreatment of a Muslim community in Myanmar. So, that was the basis on which, in 2019, the case began. It’s run for seven years. It’s been fiercely litigated. Myanmar participated very actively. At one stage, Aung San Suu Kyi, was the former Nobel Prize winner, was the head of their delegation in one of the early phases of the case. And the judgment was handed down yesterday by the International Court of Justice. And by a majority, as you said, of 9 to 6, the court found, for the first time ever — it’s a historic judgment — that a state, Myanmar, was responsible for perpetrating acts of genocide. And this has enormous significance, because it essentially breathes life into a convention that was adopted in 1948 at the instance of another single individual, Raphael Lemkin, a Polish jurist, who invented the concept of genocide in 1945. AMY GOODMAN : So, it was a 9-to-6 ruling. How does it get enforced? And then, as we begin to wrap up, talk about what this means for another case brought before the International Court of Justice by an African country, by South Africa, against Israel. They are charging Israel with genocide for what’s happened in Gaza. PHILIPPE SANDS : Well, the judgment of yesterday is binding and final, so there is no appeal. It will be enforced through U.N. bodies and, presumably, will go to the Security Council of the U.N. for some sort of authorization. But more significantly, for the first time in its history, the court has set up a process for restitution and reparation for the members of the Rohingya community. It’s given Myanmar two years to report on the steps it’s going to take to allow full restitution for the homes — but a lot of them have been destroyed, so it’s very difficult to see how that’s going to happen — and return of the Rohingya — and they may not want to return. And after two years, The Gambia will be able to go back to court and ask for reparations, not for itself, but for the individual members of the Rohingya group. So, a process is now in train and is now underway in relation to the process. In terms of the implications of the case for other cases, including the one brought by South Africa against Israel, the court has basically adopted the standard it has always adopted. To prove genocide, you have to show genocidal conduct, conduct in which the only reasonable inference is that it was motivated by an intention to destroy a group in whole or in part. And so, the burden will be on South Africa to do that with its own evidence. I’m not expressing a view as to whether that evidence meets the burden or not. But the court in the Rohingya case did go out of its way to make clear that every case will turn on its own facts. So, following this judgment yesterday, the door remains open to the South African case. It has not been shut, nor has it been opened more widely. It will be for South Africa to persuade the judges on the basis of the evidence. And just so that your viewers are clear, this case is not going to finally come to court for the major hearing for three or four years, because it’s on a very slow-track process. So don’t expect any action until 2030 or 2031. AMY GOODMAN : Finally, if you could talk about the U.S. and the China response to this decision, Philippe Sands. PHILIPPE SANDS : I mean, the initial U.S. response, the State Department put out a perfectly reasonable statement saying that they were going to study the judgment and then consider what their reaction is to it. There had been previously a tweet, I think it was, put out by the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, warning the court — almost seen by some as a threat to the court — that if it lowered the standard, it would face the same kinds of sanctions and difficulties, or might, that the International Criminal Court has faced. My own view is, as I said in the op-ed piece in The New York Times this morning, is the standard has not been lowered. The case simply turned on its own facts. It’s the same “only reasonable inference” standard. And we will have to wait and see. As for China, I’m not aware of what the reaction has been. One of the six who voted against the judgment was the Chinese judge, Madam Xue. The American judge voted in favor — AMY GOODMAN : Philippe Sands, I want to thank — PHILIPPE SANDS : — of the judgment. AMY GOODMAN : I want to thank you so much for being with us, Philippe Sands, human rights lawyer, served on The Gambia’s legal team in The Gambia v. Myanmar case at the International Court of Justice. We’ll link to your New York Times piece , “Can a Country Be Guilty of Genocide? Finally, the Answer Is Yes.” And Maung Zarni, Burmese dissident and co-author of the study , “The Slow-Burning Genocide of Myanmar’s Rohingya.” Coming up, today is the last scheduled day of the U.N. climate summit here in Antalya, Turkey. There is a great deal of controversy, advocates saying the draft agreement text is a failure and should be rejected. And the minister of Panama has said he may block the agreement if Panama’s limited demands are not met. We’ll hear from him and host a discussion with environmental justice advocates. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Polluters Must Pay” protesters dressed up as peanuts, holding up giant pennies that spell out “pay up” here at COP31 in Antalya earlier this week.

articles.title: “A COP of Betrayal”: U.N. Talks Make No Progress on Fossil Fuel Phaseout, Climate Finance
articles.content: In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change. “This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries. “At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, 'There is no money at home.' But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

articles.title: “Little Hands, Big Change”: 8-Year-Old Kenyan Climate Champion Marren Akeyo Speaks Out at COP31
articles.content: At the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026, Marren Akeyo, addressed world leaders on their responsibility to take real action to stop climate change. “Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet?” said 8-year-old Akeyo. “We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, ’You’re the leaders of tomorrow.’ Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.”

articles.title: Justice for Palestine Must Include Climate Justice: Abeer Al-Butmeh of Friends of the Earth Palestine
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. We’re in Antalya, Turkey, at U.N. climate summit, COP31. Our guest, Abeer Al-Butmeh, coordinator of PENGON , the Palestinian Environmental NGO Network, a member of Friends of the Earth International. Welcome to Democracy Now! , Abeer. ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Thank you so much. ANJALI KAMAT : Abeer, can you talk about how the climate crisis that’s being talked about here at COP31 is connected to what’s going on on the ground in Palestine? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. Climate crisis in Palestine is not natural phenomena. It’s a climate justice issue. It’s a human right issue. When we talk about justice for Palestinians, it means the sovereignty on our land, sovereignty on water resources, sovereignty on natural resources. We cannot talk about climate justice without the right for Palestinians to reach their agricultural land and to move freely between cities. We cannot talk about climate justice without the right to cope with climate changes. We need sovereignty to deal with our Palestinian water resources, that Israel has denied the access and sovereignty on all natural resources in Palestine. When we talk about climate crisis, we focus more on water resources, which is under the Israeli control. More than 85% of Palestinian water resources are under Israeli control and pumped and supplied to the Israeli illegal settlements in the West Bank. And the situation in the Gaza Strip, water was used as a weapon against the Palestinians since the beginning of the war against Gaza Strip. And other sector, which is agricultural areas, also there is no Palestinian sovereignty on the land. Currently, the Israeli settlers’ violence against the Palestinian farmers and the Palestinian organizations also are accelerated, with the protection of the Israeli forces. This is the situation in the West Bank, and while the situation in Gaza Strip is much catastrophic. Based on the statistics, only 3% of the agricultural land under accessibility for Palestinians, and you can imagine how only 3%, while before 7th of October, the agriculture sector was the main sector for people in Gaza, even it was many restrictions and restrictions on access also on the agricultural land before 7th of October. But the situation now has become unbelievable. ANJALI KAMAT : And, Abeer, you’re based in the West Bank. ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. ANJALI KAMAT : But when you’ve been here speaking, you’ve talked about what’s happening in Gaza as an ecocide. ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. ANJALI KAMAT : Can you talk about what that means? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yes, it is ecocide. Since the beginning of the war, they targeted all the elements of life inside Gaza. They cut off water, cut off energy, cut off food. That means killing of all people inside Gaza. When we talk about how it is ecocide, they damaged all the environmental sectors inside Gaza. They deliberately targeted all the environmental sectors. They targeted the agricultural areas. They targeted the wastewater treatment plants. Currently, six of the treatment plants out of service, so the raw wastewater flow without treatments to the agricultural areas and penetrate to the water reservoirs inside Gaza, which is already polluted before the war, but that mean that situation is much catastrophic. So, also they targeted the desalination plants. They targeted all the infrastructure inside Gaza. Another silent threat, which is the accumulation of solid waste beside the displaced areas, which is also the — leached for the solid waste penetrate to the soil and also reach the water wells inside Gaza Strip. In addition to that, the huge amount of debris that is mixed with heavy metals and poisonous materials. AMY GOODMAN : The debris all over the ground from the rubble? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah, yeah. So, the debris also, which is a critical concern for people inside Gaza. So, when we talk about how it is ecocide, yes, it is ecocide, killing all the components of environmental sector inside Gaza, in addition to the fishering sector. More than 95% of this sector was targeted and damaged as a result of this war, and which is the main sector for people who depend on inside Gaza. AMY GOODMAN : There is a lot of solidarity expressed here at many different actions that do not involve Palestine, but people talk about Palestine. ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. AMY GOODMAN : If you can talk about the importance of that? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah, solidarity for Palestine is very important. And it is not only a word. For people who suffer from killing, from targeting from Israel, feeling that the world support this population, that means a lot. And it is not a little, because when we feel that we are alone, that make us cannot continue our struggle. AMY GOODMAN : And, Abeer, if you can talk about your own background in the West Bank, where you grew up? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. AMY GOODMAN : Talk about the olive trees. ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah, I grew up in a village called Battir village, and I’m strongly connected with the land. Since I am a child, I was going to the agricultural areas, and I used to go to irrigate our crops. And I grew up between the mountains, between the plants. So I studied water and environmental engineer. And I’m really happy and feel myself on the ground between the agricultural areas. That’s why I see that it is very important for any Palestinian to defend the land. It is our identity, our life. So, this is — yeah, my aim is to protect my land and to raise the Palestinians’ voices among people, among international communities, to raise their demands at international spaces. ANJALI KAMAT : You know, we’re seeing so many Palestinians being cut off from their lands in the West Bank — ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. ANJALI KAMAT : — because of increased settler and soldiers, military activity, and, of course, the ecocide, as you talked about, in Gaza. A lot of the developing countries here at the COP31 are talking about loss and damages, right? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. ANJALI KAMAT : And what rich countries owe the Global South. What kind of accountability are you calling for here at COP31? ABEER AL- BUTMEH : Yeah. When we talk about climate, and we are at COP31, and we will talk about loss and damage and climate finance, the main question should be raised is how the governments can supply this ecocide happening without accountability, can finance the military for Israel. Without supporting governments, Israel cannot continue this ecocide, without supporting and the cooperation with the corporations that’s fueling this ecocide. How these governments does find finance and support for Israel to continue this ecocide, while cannot find money to support the Palestinian farmers and protecting the Palestinian farmers? This year, most of the Palestinian farmers cannot reach their agricultural land. Currently, we have the olive harvesting season. We cannot reach our groves in order to harvest. The Israeli — unfortunately, it is really painful when we see the Israeli settlers on our land harvest our trees, steal our olive oil. So, we cannot imagine how the governments, how the international community stay silent while the Israeli occupation and the Israeli settlers, with the Israeli — with the protection of the Israeli forces, continue their violations and their environmental crimes. AMY GOODMAN : Abeer Al-Butmeh, we want to thank you so much for being with us, coordinator of PENGON , the Palestinian Environmental NGO Network, a member of Friends of the Earth International, here at COP31, the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

articles.title: Seeds and Seedbeds: Two Venezuelan Initiatives for Science for Life
articles.author: Authors and Editor
articles.content: A group of farmers runs a potato-seed laboratory in Mucuchíes, in the Venezuelan state of Mérida, 3,600 metres above sea level. The Ministry of Science and Technology (Mincyt) describes this laboratory, the Biotechnology Centre for Training in Agamic Seed Production (Cebisa), as the most advanced of its kind in the country. In April 2025, the government formally handed over expanded training facilities to Cebisa, which has operated since 2009. [1] A few weeks later, on 2 May, more than 250 children and young people from ten municipalities in Zulia presented 100 robotics projects designed to solve problems in their local communities. [2] Initiatives of this kind exist in other Global South countries. What sets these apart is their context: the Venezuelan state has incorporated them into a national project, and that project stems from a question posed by Hugo Chávez: what is the purpose of each technology? [3] For Chávez, that question could not be answered within the confines of laboratories. A national development project could not succeed, he argued, unless it conceived, designed, and built its own scientific and technological approach. In Venezuela, this project took on institutional form in 1999, when Chávez came to power. The Scientific-Peasant Alliance and the National Scientific Seedbeds Programme (Semilleros) are two of its manifestations: one sows seeds, the other sows vocations. By bringing farmers and young people into scientific work, these initiatives also raise another question: who is recognised as a producer of knowledge, and who decides? What Kind of Science? For What Purpose, and Who Produces It? In June 2007, speaking to a group of grassroots inventors, Hugo Chávez acknowledged that Venezuela needed technological mastery for reasons of sovereignty and security. However, recalling the Argentine scientist Oscar Varsavsky, he added that the primary problem was not ‘know-how’ but ‘know-what’. Technology, he argued, should be neither an end in itself nor a commodity, but a means to meet needs. He concluded: ‘we have an obligation to understand the purpose of every technology’. [4] Varsavsky (1920–1976) devoted much of his work to a question that was uncomfortable for his profession: who decides what is researched and for what purpose? In Science, Politics and Scientism , he argued that the science of his time was not neutral but adapted to the social system that funded and organised it. He described ‘scientism’ as the attitude of researchers who adapted to this scientific market, ceased to concern themselves with the social significance of their work, and adopted the norms and values of the major international centres. For him, the decisive task was to set the research topics, assign priorities, and organise the work around the needs of social change. [5] In Towards a National Science Policy (1972), he extended the argument to the realm of public policy. If a country framed its scientific development as ‘closing the gap’ with advanced nations, he warned, it effectively smuggled in the essence of their way of life. Every societal project, by contrast, required its own scientific and technological approach. [6] What Varsavsky termed ‘scientism’ has a longer history. Modern science took shape alongside capitalism and Europe’s colonial expansion from the 16th century onwards, with methods, values, and perspectives that this expansion imposed on the world as universal. It rested on a division between two planes of knowledge: that which distinguishes the true from the false, and that which distinguishes right from wrong. The former was taken to be objective knowledge and became science. The latter was assigned to the subjective realm of ethics. Modern science was thus constructed in isolation from ethics. It declared itself objective and neutral, and proclaimed itself the only valid form of knowledge. It has undoubtedly brought great advances for humanity. Yet, alongside unprecedented scientific and technological development, humanity’s major problems – inequality, poverty, hunger, disease, and environmental crisis – persist, and the way science is put to use has helped deepen some of them. This contradiction is rooted in the economic and political relations within which science develops. Under capitalism, the accumulation of capital shapes research priorities, funding, the ownership of results, and the direction of innovation. Knowledge becomes a commodity, produced for expected profit rather than collective need. The starkest example is that of weapons. On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel went to war against Iran and, on the very first day, an attack on a girls’ primary school in Minab killed more than 160 people, most of them children. Behind attacks such as this stand scientists and engineers trained at universities and research centres, working for military establishments and the corporations that supply them, and increasingly using artificial intelligence systems. Discussing the wider role of AI in military targeting, Bappa Sinha describes how Palantir’s Maven system aggregates satellite imagery, drone footage, and signals intelligence to prioritise targets and recommend weaponry. With the Pentagon’s own mantra that ‘speed wins’, he argues, the time taken to verify whether a building is a school or a barracks tends towards zero. [7] Technical capability does not explain itself: it depends on who organises it and what agenda it serves. That is the distinction Chávez drew: technological mastery for reasons of sovereignty and security is one thing; technology placed at the service of a superpower’s agenda over other peoples is quite another. As he said in 2006, ‘there is no such thing as neutral science’. He argued that anyone who conducts research and claims not to be involved in politics is, in fact, involved in politics, because their work may strengthen the dominant system. [8] The first question is ‘what for?’: which problems should science address, and for whose benefit? Answering it also requires asking who sets research priorities and controls the resources. The direction of science is not fixed: it can be contested and transformed, and with it, science policy. The other question is who produces knowledge and who recognises it as valid. The presentation to Mincyt’s 2025 collection of Chávez’s speeches asks: is modern science ‘above peasant knowledge, ancestral knowledge, or popular knowledge’? How can we ensure that ‘the frameworks of knowledge of the wretched of the world and of history’ are upheld and respected? The answer is a science that is ‘community-based, participatory, diverse, and in solidarity with the oppressed’, a ‘science of the people – that is, of subalternity’ – rooted in life or, in Chávez’s words, ‘for life, for happiness’. The presentation also warns against ‘the academic trap’: declaring a different kind of science does not eliminate the geopolitics of knowledge, which is ‘a real struggle’. [9] The science that is needed does not abandon rigour, nor does it have different laws of nature: those have no nationality. What changes is who asks the questions and what the answers are used for. Chávez described it as a dialectical process whose synthesis is the interaction of popular knowledge with academic knowledge. [10] The in vitro laboratory does not compete with the memory of those who preserve native potatoes in the páramo, the high Andean grassland above the tree line; they need one another. This does not mean setting modern science aside. It means taking seriously what peasants and Indigenous peoples have learned over generations about seeds, soils, and plants – knowledge that colonial rule dismissed as backward and that capital has often appropriated – and testing it with the same rigour as any other claim. Science and the National Project Varsavsky argued that a society’s scientific and technological ‘style’ should grow out of its national project. That style would guide the organisation of research and the choice of technologies, providing the basis for specific technological strategies. [11] Chávez likewise linked technological choices to the society Venezuela sought to build. In April 2008, he rejected the idea of bridging the technological gap, arguing that this ambition meant adopting the ‘Northern project’, which he accused of putting science at the service of inequality and exploitation between countries. Venezuela had to build, not imitate. ‘It is not a question of bridging any gap; it is a question of building, of inventing’ a ‘highly dynamic, highly diverse’ style. That style, he specified, must come ‘from our very core, from our history, our culture, our traditions’ and be driven ‘by our needs’. [12] He also set out the needs this style should serve. ‘We need a scientific-technological style to achieve our food security and sovereignty, and holistic human development’ – that is to say, education, health, housing, and ‘meeting the fundamental needs of the people’. [13] But a distinctive style depends on the political choice about the society to be built. Varsavsky saw scientific autonomy as both a prerequisite for developing and carrying out a country’s own national project and a consequence of that process. [14] In Venezuela, political change made it possible to turn this approach to science into public policy. Venezuela: Two Sowings When Hugo Chávez took office, Venezuela’s public science sector depended on the National Council for Scientific and Technological Research (Conicit), which funded research projects. Chávez described the situation before 1999 in two sentences: science ‘was reserved for an elite’ and science and technology ‘were hijacked’. What had to change, in his words, was what science and technology were for: they ‘must be formidable instruments, not for the domination of minorities over majorities but, above all, for the liberation of majorities through knowledge, through scientific and technological research and its application to the social battle, to social development’. [15] The institutional change was swift. In the first year of government, the Ministry of Science and Technology was established. The Constitution approved by a referendum in December 1999 incorporated science, technology, and innovation for the first time as matters of public interest (art. 110) and required the state to guarantee the ethical principles governing research. [16] In 2000, a programme of productive cooperation networks – later renamed productive innovation networks – was launched to link rural producers with the research capacity of universities and specialist centres. In 2001, the Organic Law on Science, Technology, and Innovation (LOCTI), issued by decree, repealed the 1984 Conicit Act and transformed Conicit into the National Fund for Science, Technology, and Innovation (Fonacit). The law has since been reformed four times, in 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2022. [17] Following the enactment of the LOCTI, research priorities shifted from individual disciplines, such as physics, chemistry, and biology, towards problems concerning food, health, energy, the environment, and education. A style of science was promoted that sought to generate knowledge to construct a socially, politically, economically, and culturally just, equitable, and sustainable society. This reflected Varsavsky’s argument that science must develop from its own roots to overcome its peripheral position. Beginning with its first version in 2001 and developing through successive reforms, the law recognised traditional, ancestral, and popular knowledge and progressively broadened participation in scientific work to include communes and organised popular power. [18] Support extended beyond academic activity to projects arising from popular power, such as the Socialist Networks for Productive Innovation. Through these networks, organised groups of producers tested innovations to increase the production of food, goods, or services. Particular emphasis was placed on networks linking different stages of research, disciplines, and institutions. Antivenom research illustrates this approach: studies of snake distribution were linked to research into venom properties, the development of antivenoms, and their production. A single network brought together taxonomy, biochemistry, immunology, and drug development and production. In 2021, researchers at the Institute for Advanced Studies Foundation (IDEA) and the Francisco de Miranda University were developing antivenoms for snake and scorpion bites. [19] These connections show how planning and cooperation can direct scientific work towards public needs, treating knowledge as the heritage of the people rather than a commodity. Since 2003, the government has also turned to the ‘missions’, programmes operating alongside traditional institutions to address urgent needs in health, literacy, and university education. In 2006, the Science Mission was launched to integrate social and institutional actors into networks to generate and disseminate knowledge. In 2011, the Great Agro-Venezuela Mission set out to strengthen national food production with scientific and technological support. The Science Mission was the precursor to the ‘Dr Humberto Fernández-Morán’ Great Mission for Science, Technology and Innovation, which President Nicolás Maduro presented on 10 April 2024. Its five pillars included developing and preserving national scientific talent, and applying science, technology, and innovation for production. The Scientific-Peasant Alliance formed part of science policy supporting food production, while the Semilleros fell under the first pillar. Food sovereignty was one of the areas where the Alliance put this approach to science into practice. The Seed: The Scientific-Peasant Alliance According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the world produces enough food to feed everyone. Hunger therefore raises questions about what is produced, using which technologies, and how it is distributed. [20] The companies that promoted the Green Revolution through commercial seeds, fertilisers, and pesticides gained influence over what and how much to sow, how to distribute the harvests, and whom to finance. Seed patents and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) later became part of this system of corporate control. Within this framework, food is a commodity: it is worth whatever it can be exchanged for. The foundations laid since 1999 enabled Venezuela to respond to the food crisis caused by the unilateral coercive measures imposed on the country. Mincyt and the Corporation for Scientific and Technological Development (Codecyt) could bring universities together and fund their work, drawing on the experience of socio-productive networks. In 2013, Codecyt joined the Association of Integrated Producers of the Páramo (Proinpa), a group of producers from Mérida, to scale up the socio-productive networks. Mincyt’s 2025 publication, Alianza Científico-Campesina , records a 2014 decision to stop importing potato seed to strengthen national production. According to the publication, the subsequent intensification of the blockade prevented purchases on the international market, exposing the vulnerability of a food system reliant on imports and increasing the urgency of domestic seed production. The 2015 Seeds Act, which recognised the strategic importance of seeds for agricultural production, strengthened the legal framework for this work. [21] When seed imports became impossible, the Alliance could draw on that work to produce pre-basic seed of different varieties. By January 2016, both organisations were publicly using the name ‘Scientific-Peasant Alliance’. The Alliance grew out of earlier ministry work on socio-productive networks, among which Proinpa and others had made significant progress in organising producers and developing specific productive projects. Without these laws, institutions, and networks, a group of producers from the páramo region would hardly have had access to the laboratory facilities, resources, and recognition needed to produce seed on a national scale. [22] Through seed banks, in vitro cultivation, agroecology, and networks linking communities and universities, the Alliance brings together their knowledge and resources for production. Cebisa, the laboratory in Mucuchíes, is its most visible manifestation. The Mincyt book that systematises the Alliance’s experience highlights cases such as that of Bernabé Torres, a 64-year-old farmer who takes part in the Alliance and whom it calls the guardian of native potatoes. He recounted how the Alliance and the University of Los Andes had supported the rescue and propagation of local and native seeds, and said that without science they would be nothing, because those who did not use it were filling the land with chemicals. For Torres, the work he and his fellow farmers were doing there was ‘the future of this country’. [23] Recognition has also come from abroad: in 2026, the FAO named María Cantalicia Torres, a rural leader and seed guardian from the Venezuelan Andes, one of its 100 heroes in agrifood systems for her work recovering native potato varieties. According to the account of the experience that Mincyt has published, by 2024, the Alliance had planted more than 30,000 hectares in accordance with its guidelines across all its crop sectors (potatoes, cocoa, coffee, maize, and others), involving more than 3,500 families in 18 states. The same account, in its epilogue, adds that the Alliance now propagates more than 150 varieties of potato seed, nearly 80 of them native to the Andes, and that its locally produced seed supports potato cultivation in more than 80% of the country’s federal entities. It also reports that Cebisa saves the country more than US$460 million a year in imports. [24] The Alliance builds partnerships between farmers and scientists to advance food sovereignty, and farmers’ knowledge helps determine which seeds are propagated. Families collect and select the seeds with the greatest potential from their own territories and send them to laboratories for classification and improvement before they are returned. In practice, this is the synthesis of popular wisdom and academic knowledge that Chávez proposed. Community assemblies and conversations in the field, where producers who have worked with the Alliance share their experience, are one of the ways the approach reaches other farming families. [25] The aim is to put the country’s talent and capabilities to work on needs found in the countryside, recognising traditional and ancestral knowledge and placing the advances of academic science at the service of the people. One interviewee in the Mincyt book identifies new demands arising from the Alliance’s expansion: strengthening its seed nuclei in each region, giving farming families comprehensive technical support, and ensuring that knowledge is effectively transferred. The interviewee also considers bringing new talent into research centres key to generating solutions suited to producers’ needs. In these challenges lies an opportunity to deepen the Alliance’s impact and establish it as a reference for linking scientific research and peasant production. [26] The Semilleros: The National Scientific Seedbeds Programme While the Alliance addresses the needs of the present, the Semilleros address the nation’s future. The programme, which the Ministry of Science and Technology has run since 2019, reflects an idea central to Chávez’s developmental model: the Bolivarian Revolution could not take ‘a leap forward without science and technology’. [27] Sustaining that model also means encouraging children and young people to pursue science and giving them opportunities to generate knowledge and solve problems. The first pillar of the Great Mission reflects this aim: sowing and preserving national scientific talent. The two programmes are not separate worlds. Even before the formal launch of the Semilleros, the Alliance had forged links with schools in Mérida, where pupils and teachers were showing an interest in agriculture, ecosystems, and seeds, and had organised educational activities in the countryside. Alicia Cáceres, a biologist and researcher and professor at the Central University of Venezuela, is quoted in the Mincyt book on the Alliance describing the children who visit its laboratories: ‘They ask questions, they take you along and tell you: “But I have a hypothesis”. Everything is impressive!’ Living alongside them, she adds, is something ‘we hadn’t had before, and now we do’. The programme also invites girls to take up science, so that they become the scientists of tomorrow. [28] The National Scientific Seedbeds Programme, promoted by Mincyt, seeks to identify, train, and protect the scientific and technological talents of the future, guide early career choices, and strengthen science education amongst children and teenagers. Among its five components are ‘productive science pathways’, which bring students into contact with settings where science is directly linked to production, and educational robotics, with centres equipped with electronics and IT laboratories. The programme, which has been running since 2019, offers several avenues for participation, including Olympiads, practical workshops, and school outreach. Outreach sessions involve entire secondary school year groups. In November 2026, 265 first-year secondary school pupils in the state of Sucre took part in activities involving microscopy, chemistry, physics, robotics, and astronomy. Another 655 pupils from the states of Portuguesa and Trujillo took part in practical workshops in June 2026. [29] According to Mincyt, the programme had already reached 562,695 children and young people in 2025. [30] At the regional stage of the Creative Robotics Olympiad in Zulia state, one young participant presented an automated system for the initial processing of cocoa pods. The project was designed to support the Zulia Institute of Technological Research (INZIT) in the production of nutritious flours. Another participant designed a robot to monitor data from a manufacturing plant in real time. [31] These projects showed young people taking ownership of scientific knowledge and technological tools to address local needs. Here, robotics went beyond programming and building machines: it became a way to explore solutions to problems in food production and manufacturing. Training new generations of scientists, engineers, and technologists also raises a question of values. Creativity, rigour, and the capacity for innovation are indispensable, but they must go hand in hand with social responsibility, dialogue, and reflection on the consequences of technological applications. Preparing people to develop sophisticated technologies must be accompanied by a public discussion of purposes and limits. It is essential to nurture a population capable of participating in these decisions regarding their use, thereby sustaining the nation’s project. The challenge is to turn participation into a career path. It is essential to ensure that those who have followed scientific pathways and attended robotics clubs go on to work in laboratories, factories, and the countryside, and that schools support this vocation through high-quality education. Another Subject, Another Purpose In Minab, a war imposed by the US and Israel killed scores of schoolchildren. In Mérida and Zulia, technical skills – measuring, cultivating, and programming – are directed towards producing seeds and training those who will continue to generate knowledge. Chávez called the producers, innovators, and scientists ‘the seeds of the new homeland’. [32] The Alliance and the Semilleros are two ways of sowing them. In October 2026, the Alliance brought together more than 300 women producers from Mérida, Táchira, and Trujillo at a regional meeting in Mucuchíes. [33] Through the Semilleros, children and young people from ten municipalities in Zulia developed robotics projects to address local needs. Political change made both programmes possible, and in 2026 they continue to operate. Their continuity depends on that framework being institutionalised through legislation, the budget, and popular power. The challenge is to secure those conditions over the long term. Neither initiative alone solves the problems facing science. Together, however, they show how public policy can expand scientific capacities, recognise new producers of knowledge, and direct innovation towards collective needs when it begins by asking what science is for. What other contexts can learn from this is not the scale or the conditions, but the approach: asking ‘what for?’ first, recognising those who produce knowledge outside the university, and training from an early stage those who will sustain the effort. For the Global South, the task is not to secure a seat at the table where the scientific ‘centre’ sets the agenda, but to set its own priorities. In an era marked by artificial intelligence and large language models, the question of who directs technology and whom it serves is even more urgent. As Sinha points out, artificial intelligence has enormous potential in healthcare, climate science, and planning for human needs; the problem is when its development and use are subordinated to the war machine. [34] The ability to process information and automate tasks does not, in itself, determine which uses should be prioritised or who will benefit from them. Such decisions require public debate and participation in setting priorities. A science for life is not a less rigorous or less advanced science. It is a science whose organisation, priorities, and applications address the question of its social purposes. Its direction and future are determined by what is researched, by who conducts the research, and by the national vision that underpins it. The decisive question is never what technology can do. It is who makes technology, and for whom. articles.title: BDS at 20: activists confront European complicity at Barcelona conference
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: “This is a European issue because Europe is a partner in crime,” co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement Omar Barghouti said on the opening day of a conference marking the movement’s 20th anniversary in Barcelona. “Most of the governments, the corporations, the institutions, the universities, your so-called media, many of them are partners in crimes. They’re complicit in Israel’s regime of genocide, apartheid, occupation – and they have been for quite some time.” Hundreds of people attended the opening night of the BDS conference in Barcelona on November 18. Source: BreakThrough News The BDS campaign has seen a notable surge in Europe since the beginning of the genocide in Gaza, supported by diverse groups, from trade unions to left political parties. “This campaign is important to confront apartheid, militarization, and genocide,” general secretary of the Workers’ Party of Belgium (PTB-PVDA) Peter Mertens told BreakThrough News at the opening. “It means working towards a future against the war machine. Defeat the war machine, defeat genocide, defeat apartheid – this will liberate not only Palestine, but all of us.” The three-day event, taking place through November 20 under the theme “Resisting Might-Makes-Right: for Palestine, for Humanity,” is organized by the Palestinian BDS National Committee (BNC), including the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI), in cooperation with European partners. Hundreds of people joined the launch event on November 18. Barghouti spoke alongside UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese , surgeon Ghassan Abu-Sittah, actress Hiba Abouk, and former Colombian energy minister Andrés Camacho. Later sessions featured human rights attorney Noura Erakat , writer Fatima Bhutto, and trade unionist Zita Holbourne, among others. BDS actions as “lights piercing the darkness of European complicity and repression” Offering a glimpse into upcoming days of strategizing and exchange by Palestine solidarity activists, the opening speakers took stock of Europe’s ongoing complicity in Israeli crimes – and of the breakthroughs achieved through BDS initiatives across the region. The movement has undeniably grown since 2023. Groups are campaigning against tech companies that fuel the genocide while embedding themselves in European public and security services. Cultural , academic, and sports boycott campaigns have expanded alongside them. Dockworkers blocked arms shipments to Israel, and students launched dozens of encampments against their universities’ cooperation with the occupation’s institutions. Read more: BDS movement makes significant strides across Europe These actions, Barghouti said, “are some of those many beautiful European lights that are shining and piercing the darkness of European complicity and repression.” “The Gaza genocide has become the litmus test by which people test the moral fabric of individuals, pop stars, and politicians,” Abu-Sittah emphasized, adding that the tone and strength of recent student demonstrations represented another achievement. Read more: Israeli destruction of Gaza’s healthcare is a blueprint for future imperialist wars “There is a generation that is formatively and structurally aware of the relationship between capitalist austerity that is destroying the lives of the people in the core of the empire and capitalist colonialism that is consuming the lives of Palestinians in Gaza through a system that also creates profit,” he said. “These cannibalistic classes of Western colonialism that consume the lives of the poor and the superfluous populations in Europe, in North America, are the cannibalistic classes that consume the lives of the children and the Palestinian civilians inside Gaza.” International law is still relevant Yet European countries continue to conduct business as usual and maintain partnerships with the occupation power, Barghouti argued, with the regional far right enthusiastically joining the drive despite its own antisemitic character. “Israel sells its military technologies as ‘battle tested’ and extensively uses bribery, bullying and extortion of elected officials including through ‘private Mossad companies,” he insisted. “Israel exports weaponized spyware and has used this information in election rigging services to influence elections in Slovenia , France, NYC, and possibly in Colombia and Brazil.” Opening speakers included Omar Barghouti, Francesca Albanese, Ghassan Abu-Sittah, Hiba Abouk, Andrés Camacho, and many more. Source: BreakThrough News In such a context, Francesca Albanese said during a press conference ahead of the launch, many ask if international law is still relevant. “Oh, yes, it is very relevant.” Instruments like the UN Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the Refugee Convention, she added, “exist to protect humanity from war, persecution, and extermination.” “I agree that the system that was conceived 80 years ago was still bearing the colonial imprint of the countries who composed the international community back then, and that we are still fighting to undo that colonial legacy. That system has not led us to heaven, but has saved us – until now – from hell.” Palestinians are calling for meaningful solidarity, not charity “International law, as we understand it, was established in order to facilitate relationships between imperial powers as they expanded their hold on the globe, its resources, and its people,” added Noura Erakat. “It was because of the Third World revolt that we saw these laws transform in order to serve us and to serve the salt of this earth.” “And so we – as those in the Third World tradition have always done – retool these tools that are meant to suppress us and to maintain the structure of domination, in order to advance justice on behalf of the people. At this moment, it is not what international law says about Palestine, but rather what Palestine says about international law and its legitimacy.” Read more: Romania: a growing hub of complicity in genocide “To resist this [might-makes-right] order, Palestinians have a near consensus in our demand to the global solidarity movement,” Barghouti said. “One, uplift the inalienable right of our people under international law, at the very least an end to the occupation, end to apartheid, and right of refugees to return and to reparations. And two, end all forms of complicity in Israeli crimes, especially through BDS.” “Palestinians are not calling for charity. We are calling for meaningful solidarity.”

articles.title: Far-right student groups attack book exhibition with crude bomb
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: A progressive book exhibition, organized by students of Calcutta University in India’s eastern state of West Bengal, faced a crude bomb attack by right-wing student organizations affiliated with the ruling ultra-right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), on Wednesday, November 18. The exhibition continued, even after the attack , which was allegedly carried out by the members of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidhyarthi Parishad (ABVP), student wing of the Hindu supremacist organization Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh or National Volunteer Union (RSS), the parent organization of the BJP. A day earlier, security forces tried to stop the same exhibition and had attacked the book stalls set up by students and arrested several activists and leaders resisting their action. The attack by the security forces had prompted big protests by students, who accused the BJP-led state government of trying to censor books and crack down on the culture of dissent. Students have accused that Wednesday’s attacks were the result of the government shielding and promoting such violence against progressive books, cultural events, and university spaces. The protesting students have also demanded the release of activists arrested by the police on Tuesday. In a statement issued by the Student Federation of India (SFI), a left-wing student organization and the main organizer of the book exhibition, called the repeated attacks an assault on “democratic rights, freedom of expression, and the long-standing traditions of intellectual and political debate” in the state. The SFI and other left student groups organize book exhibitions in Kolkata’s College Street called “Literature of Struggle” every year to commemorate the 1917 October Revolution in Russia. The SFI claimed the attacks against them were part of the larger right wing turn West Bengal has taken, but reiterated its resolve to continue its resistance, despite the attacks. Rising intolerance towards freedom of expression The attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday were a continuation of similar attacks last month when the newly-formed BJP state government deployed bulldozers to demolish traditional progressive book stalls, organized every year during religious festivities. The BJP and ABVP activists have also been accused of attacking other book stalls and of launching a systemic attack on universities and cultural events in the state under police protection. The right-wing groups allege that progressive books, university spaces, and cultural events deliberately promote “anti-national” elements and ideas and must be stopped. The left organizations have called such reasoning a reflection of the BJP’s ideological intolerance of diversity and its fear of political dissent, with some even terming it “fascistic.” On October 31, thousands of people marched across the streets of Kolkata with books in hand to register their opposition to rising attacks on universities, freedom of expression, and cultural traditions in the state. The left student groups have also made a call for fresh mobilizations against such attacks on Friday, November 20.
